faq.q: What is the best place to sell used auto parts online?
faq.a: It depends on your operation. For individual sellers with a handful of parts, eBay Motors offers the widest buyer reach at the cost of roughly 15% in fees. For salvage yards and dismantlers moving volume, Car-Part.com provides passive national exposure through inventory databases, while voice networks like Hotline HQ deliver the fastest yard-to-yard sales with 2-second average response times. Most successful yards use two or three channels together.

faq.q: How much does eBay charge to sell auto parts?
faq.a: eBay charges an insertion fee (first 250 listings per month are free for most sellers) plus a final value fee of approximately 14.35% of the sale price, including shipping, plus a $0.30 per-order surcharge. eBay Motors Parts & Accessories follows this standard fee structure. Payment processing is included in the final value fee since eBay manages payments directly.

faq.q: Can I sell used auto parts on Facebook Marketplace?
faq.a: Yes. Facebook Marketplace charges no listing fees and no commission for local pickup sales. If you use Facebook's shipping option, a 10% selling fee applies (minimum $1.00). Most used auto parts transactions on Facebook happen as local pickup due to the size and weight of parts, making it effectively free to sell there.

faq.q: Is it worth listing salvage parts on Craigslist in 2026?
faq.a: Craigslist is still free and still gets traffic, but buyer quality has declined. Expect more no-shows and lowball offers than on specialized platforms. It works best for heavy, hard-to-ship parts like engines and transmissions where local pickup is the only realistic option. For a salvage yard, the time spent managing Craigslist inquiries often outweighs the savings from zero fees.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to sell used auto parts?
faq.a: Voice hotline networks are the fastest channel for yard-to-yard sales. On the Hotline HQ network, a single broadcast reaches 100+ yards simultaneously, and the average response time is approximately 2 seconds. Online marketplaces like eBay reach more individual buyers but sales typically take days to weeks, not minutes.

faq.q: Do I need a business license to sell used auto parts online?
faq.a: Requirements vary by state. Occasional sellers typically don't need a license for selling personal vehicle parts. However, if you're regularly buying and reselling auto parts for profit, most states require a business license and potentially a salvage dealer license. Some platforms like eBay require tax information once you hit certain sales thresholds (currently $600 annually triggers a 1099-K). Check your state's Department of Motor Vehicles and revenue department for specific requirements.

posts.bodyHtml:
The best place to sell used auto parts online depends on what you're selling and how you're set up. If you run a salvage yard or dismantling operation and want speed, a voice network like Hotline HQ moves parts in seconds across 500+ connected yards. If you're an individual seller looking for the widest buyer pool, eBay Motors puts your listing in front of millions. And if you want zero fees and don't mind slower sales, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist still work for local pickup deals.

No single platform wins on every front. Fees, speed, buyer reach, and the type of parts you carry all push you toward different channels. This guide breaks down seven real options — what each one costs, how fast parts move, who's buying, and where each platform falls short. Whether you're clearing shelves at a yard or selling a transmission out of your garage, one of these fits.

*Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this guide and operates a voice hotline network (option 7 below). We've covered every platform honestly, including the trade-offs of our own.*

Key Takeaways
>
- eBay Motors offers the largest buyer reach but charges roughly 15% in combined fees - Facebook Marketplace is free for local pickup sales, but buyer quality varies widely - Car-Part.com connects you to the largest used parts database (200M+ parts) for passive, always-on exposure - Voice networks like Hotline HQ deliver the fastest sales — about 2 seconds per broadcast response - Most profitable yards and sellers use two to three channels, not just one - The right mix depends on your volume, part types, and whether you're selling yard-to-yard or direct-to-consumer

The 7 Best Places to Sell Used Auto Parts Online

The used auto parts market in the US generates an estimated $12 billion to $14 billion annually, with roughly 9,000 auto recycling businesses competing for buyers (Automotive Recyclers Association). That market supports a wide range of selling channels — from massive consumer marketplaces to specialized industry networks.

Here are the seven platforms that actually move used auto parts in 2026, ranked by the size of their buyer pool. Later, we'll break down which ones make sense for your specific situation.

For a broader look at how yards approach multi-channel selling, see our guide on how salvage yards sell more parts.

1. eBay Motors

Best for: Individual sellers and yards that want the widest consumer reach How it works: You create a listing with photos, part details, fitment data, and price. Buyers find your listing through eBay search or Google Shopping. When a part sells, you ship it or arrange local pickup. eBay handles payment processing.

eBay Motors is the 800-pound gorilla of online auto parts sales. The eBay marketplace overall sees roughly 133 million active buyers worldwide (eBay Inc., Q1 2025 earnings). The Parts & Accessories category is one of eBay's largest, and eBay Motors consistently ranks among the top results in Google for used auto parts searches.

Pricing and fees: eBay gives most sellers 250 free insertion listings per month. After that, insertion fees are typically $0.35 per listing. The final value fee runs approximately 14.35% of the total sale amount (including shipping), plus a $0.30 per-order surcharge. For a $200 transmission, you'd pay about $29 in fees after the sale closes. Speed of sale: Variable. High-demand parts from popular vehicles (Honda Civic headlights, F-150 tailgates) can sell within days. Niche parts for older or uncommon vehicles may sit for weeks or months. eBay works better as a long-tail play than a quick-sale channel. Reach: National and international. eBay's buyer pool is unmatched for consumer-facing parts sales. Buyers search by year, make, model, and part number — and eBay's fitment data system helps match your listing to the right vehicles. Pros:
  • Largest buyer pool of any platform
  • eBay's fitment tools help buyers find compatible parts
  • Built-in payment processing and buyer/seller protections
  • Strong Google Shopping and organic search visibility
  • Supports both auction and fixed-price formats
Cons:
  • Roughly 15% in fees on every sale eats into margins
  • Shipping logistics fall on you — heavy parts like engines and transmissions are expensive to ship
  • Returns and buyer disputes can be costly and time-consuming
  • Listing quality matters — poor photos and descriptions mean no sales
  • High competition from professional eBay parts sellers and large dismantlers

2. Facebook Marketplace

Best for: Local pickup sales with zero fees How it works: You post a listing with photos, description, and price. Buyers in your area browse or search Marketplace and message you directly. Transactions happen in person. There's no built-in payment processing for local sales — cash, Venmo, or Zelle are the norm.

Facebook Marketplace reaches an enormous audience. Meta reported over 3 billion monthly active users across its platforms in 2024, and Marketplace is available in most US markets. For auto parts, it works best when the buyer is within driving distance.

Pricing and fees: Zero fees for local pickup transactions. If you use Facebook's shipping option (available for some categories), a 10% selling fee applies with a $1.00 minimum. Most used auto parts transactions happen locally, so you'll typically pay nothing. Speed of sale: Fast for common, in-demand parts in populated areas. Slow or nonexistent in rural markets. Expect a lot of "Is this still available?" messages that go nowhere. Reach: Broad but local. Your listing is shown primarily to buyers within a radius you set (typically 40 to 100 miles). National reach is possible through shipping, but that defeats the main advantage of the platform. Pros:
  • No fees on local pickup sales
  • Huge local audience — almost everyone has a Facebook account
  • Easy to list from your phone with photos
  • Buyers can see your profile, which builds some trust
  • Works well for large, heavy parts that are impractical to ship
Cons:
  • No buyer verification or vetting — flaky buyers and no-shows are common
  • No fitment tools or structured parts data
  • Low-ball offers are relentless
  • No built-in payment protection for local sales
  • Listings expire and get buried quickly without re-posting
  • Not designed for auto parts — you're competing with furniture, electronics, and everything else

3. Car-Part.com

Best for: Salvage yards that want passive, always-on national exposure How it works: Yards running compatible inventory management software (especially Checkmate, which Car-Part.com owns) upload their inventory data to Car-Part.com's database. Buyers search by year, make, model, and part type. Results show which yards have the part, along with price and condition. The buyer then contacts the yard directly to arrange purchase and shipping.

Car-Part.com is the industry standard for used parts search. Over 200 million parts are searchable in their database (Car-Part.com). No other platform comes close in raw inventory size. If you run a salvage yard and you're not on Car-Part.com, you're invisible to a large chunk of the buying market.

Pricing and fees: Car-Part.com charges yards a subscription fee for listing access. Pricing varies by yard size and integration level but typically runs several hundred dollars per month. There are no per-sale commissions. For buyers, searching is free. Speed of sale: Passive. Parts sell when a buyer finds your listing and decides to call. You're not actively pushing parts — they sit in the database until someone searches for them. Speed depends on demand for the specific part and how many other yards have it listed. Reach: The largest in the used auto parts industry. The 200M+ parts database draws buyers ranging from repair shops and body shops to individual consumers doing their own repairs. For a deeper comparison of how Car-Part.com stacks up against other networks, see our platform comparison guide. Pros:
  • The largest used auto parts database in the industry
  • Standard tool that shops and buyers already know how to use
  • Passive exposure — parts sell without active effort once listed
  • No per-transaction fees
  • Integration with popular yard management software
Cons:
  • Inventory data freshness depends on how often you sync — a part sold yesterday might still show as available today
  • You need compatible inventory software to list effectively
  • Subscription costs regardless of how many parts you sell
  • Buyer contacts come in as phone calls or emails — no real-time push
  • High competition from other yards listing the same parts

For tips on setting yard pricing competitively across platforms, read our used auto parts pricing guide.

4. Craigslist

Best for: Free, no-frills local listings for heavy or hard-to-ship parts How it works: You post a classified ad with photos, a description, and your asking price. Buyers browse or search the auto parts section in their metro area. Communication happens through Craigslist's anonymized email relay or by phone number if you include one. All transactions are in person.

Craigslist has been around since 1995 and remains one of the most-visited classified sites in the US. For auto parts, it's a bare-bones option — no fitment data, no payment processing, no buyer verification.

Pricing and fees: Free. Craigslist charges nothing to post in the auto parts category in most markets. A few metro areas charge a small fee for certain categories, but parts and accessories listings are typically $0. Speed of sale: Unpredictable. You might sell a popular part the same day or re-post the same listing for months with no bites. Craigslist's audience for auto parts has shrunk as Facebook Marketplace and specialized platforms have gained ground. Reach: Local only. Each posting is tied to a specific metro area. There's no national search and no way to reach buyers outside your region. Pros:
  • Completely free
  • No account required (though one is available)
  • Simple to post — minimal barriers to listing
  • Works for large, heavy parts where local pickup is the only option
Cons:
  • Buyer quality is low — expect scam attempts, no-shows, and lowball offers
  • No structured data, fitment tools, or inventory integration
  • Listings get buried quickly and require frequent re-posting
  • No payment protection or dispute resolution
  • Declining traffic for auto parts compared to five years ago
  • No seller reputation or review system

5. PartCycle

Best for: Yards that want a B2B marketplace with lower fees than consumer platforms How it works: PartCycle connects salvage yards, recyclers, and repair shops on a wholesale-focused marketplace. Yards upload inventory and set pricing. Repair shops and other buyers search for parts and order through the platform. PartCycle handles the transaction and coordinates shipping logistics.

PartCycle positions itself as a modern alternative to older B2B parts networks. The platform focuses on quality-graded, warrantied parts and targets professional buyers — repair shops, body shops, and fleet operators — rather than individual consumers.

Pricing and fees: PartCycle charges a transaction fee on sales made through the platform. The exact rate varies by agreement, but it's generally lower than eBay's roughly 15% cut. Some yards also pay a subscription or onboarding fee. Contact PartCycle directly for current pricing. Speed of sale: Moderate. PartCycle's buyer base is smaller than eBay's or Car-Part.com's, but the buyers are professional — they know what they need and they buy without the tire-kicking you see on consumer platforms. Reach: Growing but limited compared to established platforms. PartCycle's network includes thousands of yards and repair shops, but it doesn't have the volume or name recognition of Car-Part.com or eBay. Its strongest coverage is in markets with high recycler density. Pros:
  • Lower fees than eBay for most sellers
  • Professional buyer base — less wasted time on unqualified leads
  • Quality grading and warranty support builds buyer trust
  • Shipping coordination through the platform
  • Focus on the auto recycling industry rather than general commerce
Cons:
  • Smaller buyer pool than eBay or Car-Part.com
  • Less name recognition — many shops haven't heard of PartCycle yet
  • Transaction fees still eat into margins, even if lower than eBay's
  • Requires inventory upload and platform onboarding
  • Not ideal for individual sellers — geared toward licensed yards

6. LKQ / Hollander

Best for: Yards already in the LKQ network or using Hollander interchange data How it works: LKQ Corporation is the largest buyer and reseller of recycled auto parts in North America. Hollander, which LKQ acquired, provides the interchange numbering system used across the industry to match parts across different vehicles. If you're an LKQ affiliate or supplier, parts move through their national distribution network. For independent yards, Hollander interchange numbers are essential for listing parts accurately on any platform.

LKQ operates over 800 locations across North America and generated roughly $14 billion in revenue in 2024 (LKQ Corporation, 2024 annual report). They sell to repair shops, insurance companies, and consumers. Independent yards can supply parts to LKQ as wholesale vendors.

Pricing and fees: If you sell to LKQ as a wholesale supplier, pricing is negotiated directly and typically at wholesale rates below what you'd get selling direct to shops or consumers. The trade-off is volume and speed — LKQ buys in quantity and pays reliably. Using Hollander interchange data for your own listings may involve a licensing fee depending on your yard management software. Speed of sale: Fast if you're selling wholesale to LKQ — they buy what they need and pay promptly. For parts moving through the broader LKQ retail network, speed depends on demand and location. Reach: The largest in the industry. LKQ's distribution network covers all major US markets and extends into Europe. The Hollander interchange system is the standard reference for parts interchangeability across the entire recycling industry. Pros:
  • Access to the largest auto parts distribution network in North America
  • Reliable wholesale buyer if you become an LKQ supplier
  • Hollander interchange numbers are the industry standard for parts identification
  • Volume purchasing means faster inventory turnover
  • LKQ handles logistics, distribution, and customer service on their end
Cons:
  • Wholesale pricing means lower per-part margins
  • LKQ competes with independent yards for the same buyers
  • Supplying LKQ means you're helping a competitor grow
  • Hollander data licensing costs can add up for smaller operations
  • Less control over pricing and customer relationships
  • Not a platform you "list on" — it's a supply relationship

7. Hotline HQ

Best for: Salvage yards that want the fastest yard-to-yard sales channel How it works: Hotline HQ connects over 500 salvage yards across 12 regional conference rooms on a live voice network. Your yard's desk phone stays connected to your regional room — California, Texas, Florida, Arizona, and others. When any yard on the network needs a part, they key up and describe it: "2019 Ram 1500 left headlight assembly." Every connected yard hears the request in real time. You have the part? Key up, respond, and close the deal directly. Average response time: approximately 2 seconds (Hotline HQ network data).

No database. No inventory upload. No waiting for someone to find your listing. Live voice, live response.

Pricing and fees: Flat monthly membership fee. No per-call charges, no listing fees, no per-sale commission. A preconfigured desk phone ships with your membership. For current pricing, see HotlineHQ.com. Speed of sale: The fastest of any channel covered in this guide. A broadcast goes out, every yard in the room hears it, and responses come back in seconds. There's no listing-and-wait cycle. Parts that would sit in a database for weeks move the same day on the hotline because someone, somewhere on the network, needs it right now. Reach: Over 500 yards across major US markets. Reach is regional — you hear broadcasts from yards in your room and nearby rooms. It's not a national consumer marketplace, and it doesn't replace platforms that reach individual buyers. It supplements them with a fast, direct, yard-to-yard channel.

For a full breakdown of how the network operates, see our guide on how auto parts hotlines work. For a side-by-side look at how Hotline HQ compares to other industry networks, read PartsHotlines vs. Car-Part.com vs. Hotline HQ.

Pros:
  • Fastest time-to-sale of any channel — seconds, not days
  • One broadcast reaches 100+ yards simultaneously
  • Flat monthly fee with no commissions or per-sale costs
  • No inventory upload or database management required
  • Built for the way yards already work — voice, not clicks
  • Direct yard-to-yard relationships with no middleman
Cons:
  • Yard-to-yard only — doesn't reach individual consumers
  • Regional model means coverage varies by market
  • Requires a desk phone and someone at the counter to respond
  • Not a fit for individual sellers or one-off part sales
  • Newer network — smaller than Car-Part.com's 200M+ parts database

Which Platform Fits Your Operation

Seven platforms, seven different strengths. Here's the short version of which one fits whom:

You're a salvage yard or dismantler moving volume: Start with Car-Part.com for passive national reach and Hotline HQ for fast yard-to-yard sales. These two cover different needs and complement each other well. Add eBay Motors if you have the staff to manage listings and ship parts to individual buyers. You're a small yard with limited staff: Hotline HQ requires the least overhead — no inventory uploads, no listing management, just listen and respond. Car-Part.com adds passive exposure if your yard management software supports it. You're an individual selling a few parts: eBay Motors gives you the widest audience. Facebook Marketplace works for local pickup of large parts. Craigslist is free but slower and riskier. You want the lowest fees possible: Facebook Marketplace (free for local) and Craigslist (free) cost nothing. Hotline HQ's flat fee means no per-sale hit. eBay's roughly 15% fee is the most expensive option. You want the fastest sale: Hotline HQ. Nothing else in this industry matches a 2-second response on a live voice broadcast. Everything else — eBay, Facebook, Car-Part.com — involves waiting for someone to find your listing and decide to reach out.

To understand how pricing affects which channel works best for different parts, check our used auto parts pricing guide. For data on which parts generate the most demand across these platforms, see the most-requested used auto parts.

Why One Channel Isn't Enough

The yards that consistently move the most inventory don't rely on a single platform. They stack channels. A typical high-volume yard might run Car-Part.com for passive database exposure, Hotline HQ for real-time yard-to-yard sales, and eBay Motors for direct-to-consumer sales on high-margin parts.

Each channel solves a different problem. Car-Part.com catches buyers who search. Hotline HQ catches buyers who broadcast. eBay catches consumers who Google. Facebook catches locals who browse.

The risk of relying on one channel is obvious: if eBay raises fees, if Car-Part.com's data gets stale, if Facebook changes its algorithm, your sales drop overnight. Two or three channels give you redundancy and reach different buyer types.

Start with the channel that matches how your operation already works. If you have good inventory data, add Car-Part.com. If you have a counter person who can respond quickly, add Hotline HQ. If you have someone who can photograph and list parts, add eBay. Then expand from there.

For a deeper look at building a multi-channel sales strategy, read our guide on how salvage yards sell more parts. And if you want to understand how buyers on the other side find your parts across these channels, see our guide to finding used auto parts online. You can also explore our main sell used auto parts page for a quick overview of how Hotline HQ fits into your selling workflow.

faq.q: How do I find a junkyard or salvage yard near me?
faq.a: Start with a Google Maps search for "junkyard near me" or "salvage yard near me." Filter by rating and hours. Then check Car-Part.com's yard locator and your state's automotive recycler association directory for licensed facilities that might not rank well in Google. For hard-to-find parts, a voice network like Hotline HQ can broadcast your request to 100+ yards at once across your region.

faq.q: What is the difference between a junkyard, a salvage yard, and an auto recycler?
faq.a: They are largely the same thing. "Junkyard" is the informal term, "salvage yard" is more industry-standard, and "auto recycler" is the professional designation used by trade groups like the Automotive Recyclers Association. Self-service yards (also called u-pull-it or pick-a-part) let you remove parts yourself. Full-service yards pull, test, and sometimes warranty the part for you.

faq.q: Are used auto parts from salvage yards reliable?
faq.a: Most parts from licensed salvage yards work fine. Full-service recyclers typically test components like engines and transmissions and offer 30 to 90 day warranties. Mechanical parts carry more risk than body panels or glass. Ask about return policies before you buy, and inspect the part in person when possible.

faq.q: How much cheaper are salvage yard parts compared to new?
faq.a: Used parts from salvage yards generally cost 40 to 60 percent less than new OEM parts, and 20 to 40 percent less than aftermarket equivalents. Prices vary by part type, demand, and region. Engines and transmissions see the biggest savings in dollar terms. Body panels and interior trim are often available at steep discounts because supply outpaces demand.

faq.q: Should I call ahead before visiting a salvage yard?
faq.a: Yes. Call ahead with the year, make, model, and part name. The yard can check whether they have the vehicle in stock and whether the part has already been pulled. This saves you a wasted trip. Many full-service yards will pull and hold the part for you if you are on your way.

faq.q: Can I search multiple salvage yards at once for a specific part?
faq.a: Yes. Car-Part.com searches thousands of yards' inventories simultaneously. Voice networks like Hotline HQ broadcast your part request to 100+ connected yards in real time, so you get live responses rather than database listings that may be outdated. Both methods are far more efficient than calling yards one by one.

Finding used auto parts near you comes down to knowing where to look and which method fits the part you need. If you want something common, a local self-service junkyard will usually have it for cheap. If you need a specific part for a specific year and model, searching multiple yards at once through a database or voice network will save you hours of phone calls. Six reliable methods exist, and most people who do this regularly use at least two.

This guide covers every practical way to locate salvage yards and used parts in your area, what to expect when you visit, and how to decide between going local and searching online. If you already know you want to search remotely, our companion guide covers how to find used auto parts online in detail.

Key Takeaways
>
- Google Maps is the fastest way to find nearby yards, but it misses smaller unlisted operations - Car-Part.com's yard locator covers 3,500+ recyclers across North America - State recycler associations list licensed facilities that meet environmental and quality standards - Voice networks like Hotline HQ broadcast your request to 100+ yards simultaneously for real-time answers - Self-service yards save the most money; full-service yards save the most time - California, Texas, Florida, and Arizona have the highest concentrations of salvage yards in the US

Six Ways to Find Used Auto Parts Near You

Roughly 9,000 auto recycling facilities operate across the United States, according to the Automotive Recyclers Association (ARA, 2024). No single search method reaches all of them, so your best move is knowing which tool to reach for depending on what you need.

Here are the six methods, ordered from simplest to most powerful:

  1. Google Maps and local search -- fast, visual, good for finding what's close
  2. Car-Part.com yard finder -- the largest recycler directory, searchable by location
  3. State recycler associations -- vetted, licensed facilities with quality standards
  4. Hotline HQ regional rooms -- live voice broadcast to 100+ yards at once
  5. Craigslist and Facebook groups -- free, unstructured, hit-or-miss
  6. Direct phone calls -- old-fashioned but effective for one or two local yards

Most people start with Google Maps. That gets you addresses, hours, and reviews. But it only scratches the surface. The methods further down this list unlock yards that don't invest in their online presence but carry exactly the part you need.

Google Maps and Local Search

The quickest way to find a salvage yard near you is to open Google Maps and search "junkyard near me," "salvage yard near me," or "used auto parts near me." Google pulls up a map with pins, ratings, phone numbers, hours, and directions.

This works well for getting oriented. You'll see which yards are closest, which ones have decent reviews, and which ones are open right now. For common parts on common vehicles, this might be all you need. Pick the closest yard with 4+ stars, call ahead, and drive over.

Where Google Maps falls short is coverage. Smaller yards, especially rural operations, often don't have a Google Business Profile or rank poorly in local search. A yard 15 miles away with exactly the part you need might not show up because a bigger operation closer to you dominates the results.

Also, Google won't tell you whether a specific yard has your part. It tells you the yard exists. You still need to call.

Tips for better local search results

  • Search for the specific part type: "used transmission shop near me" or "salvage engines near me" sometimes surfaces specialty yards
  • Expand the map radius manually by zooming out, then browsing pins outside your immediate area
  • Check Google reviews for mentions of the vehicle make you need -- reviewers often mention specific brands a yard specializes in
  • Look at the "People also search for" suggestions at the bottom of results for nearby yards Google didn't initially show

Car-Part.com Yard Finder

Car-Part.com is best known as a parts search engine indexing over 200 million parts (Car-Part.com, 2025), but it also functions as the most comprehensive salvage yard directory in North America. Their yard locator lets you search by state and city to find recyclers in your area, along with contact information and what inventory systems they use.

This is more useful than Google Maps in two ways. First, it lists yards that specifically participate in the recycling network, meaning they actively manage inventory and are more likely to be able to tell you what they have in stock. Second, you can search their inventory directly on the same site. Find the yard, then search it for your part.

If you're looking for a specific part and want to cast a wide net, Car-Part.com's inventory search will show you results from yards across the country, not just nearby ones. But for a "near me" search, their directory helps you discover local facilities you might not find through Google alone.

State Recycler Associations

Every major state has an automotive recycler association that maintains a directory of member yards. These are licensed, inspected facilities that agree to environmental standards and, in most cases, offer some form of warranty on parts.

Here are the associations for the states with the highest yard density:

  • California: California Automotive Wholesalers' Association (CAWA) and various regional groups cover the state's 800+ recyclers
  • Texas: Texas Automotive Recyclers Association (TARA) lists members across the state's major metro areas
  • Florida: Florida Automotive Dismantlers and Recyclers Association (FADRA) covers one of the densest used-parts markets in the Southeast
  • Arizona: Arizona Automotive Recyclers Association maintains a directory of desert-climate yards known for rust-free body parts

Why does the association listing matter? Because a yard that pays dues and submits to inspections is more likely to operate professionally, price fairly, and honor a return. That's not a guarantee. But it filters out fly-by-night operations that buy wrecks, strip the easy parts, and leave you with no recourse if something is wrong.

For state-specific yard directories and part availability, see our pages for California, Texas, Florida, and Arizona.

Hotline HQ Regional Rooms

*Disclosure: Hotline HQ is our product. We'll explain what it does and let you decide if it fits.*

Hotline HQ is a voice parts network that connects yards across regional "rooms." When a member yard needs a part, they broadcast the request and every connected yard in that room hears it in real time. If someone has the part, they respond within seconds. No searching. No waiting for email replies. No stale database listings.

The network currently operates active rooms in California, Texas, Florida, and Arizona, with coverage expanding. It's designed for speed and for parts that are hard to find through traditional search. Where databases show you what was in stock last time someone updated a listing, a voice broadcast confirms what's actually available right now.

This method works best when you need a part fast, when you're looking for something uncommon, or when you've already struck out on Car-Part.com and want a real-time check across multiple yards. For a deeper look at how voice-based parts sourcing works, read our guide on how auto parts hotlines work.

If you're an individual car owner rather than a yard, Hotline HQ is primarily a yard-to-yard network. But you can ask your local repair shop or salvage yard if they're on the network and can broadcast a request on your behalf.

Craigslist, Facebook Groups, and Forums

Free options exist, and they work -- sometimes. Craigslist auto parts listings show what's available in your immediate area. Facebook Marketplace and local auto parts groups can surface deals from people parting out vehicles in their driveways. Car-specific forums (model-year forums, enthusiast boards) are especially useful for older or specialty vehicles where salvage yard coverage is thin.

The downside is time. You're scrolling through unstructured listings with inconsistent descriptions, no standardized pricing, and no warranty. Scam listings appear regularly on all three platforms. There is no way to search 50 yards at once the way you can with Car-Part.com or a voice network.

When Craigslist and Facebook groups are worth your time:

  • You're looking for a cheap, common part and you're not in a rush
  • You need a part for an older or specialty vehicle (pre-1990, import, performance car) that salvage yards may have already crushed
  • You're parting out your own vehicle and want to see local pricing before you list
  • You live in a rural area with few salvage yards within driving distance

When they're not worth the effort:

  • You need the part today or tomorrow
  • You need a verified, warrantied component
  • You're sourcing for a shop and need consistent supply

Self-Service vs Full-Service Yards

Salvage yards fall into two broad categories, and knowing the difference before you visit saves time and frustration.

Self-service yards (u-pull-it / pick-a-part)

You walk the lot, find the vehicle, and remove the part yourself. Pricing is standardized -- most self-service yards use a fixed price list based on part type, not vehicle make or model. An alternator costs the same whether it came off a Civic or a Camry.

Self-service yards charge the lowest prices in the industry. Expect to pay 50 to 70 percent less than retail salvage prices. The trade-off is labor: you need your own tools, you need to know how to remove the part without breaking it, and the experience can be physically demanding, especially in summer heat or winter cold.

Major self-service chains include LKQ Pick Your Part, Pull-A-Part, and Ecology Auto Parts. Most metro areas have at least one independent u-pull-it yard as well.

Full-service yards

The yard pulls the part for you. They typically test it, clean it, and offer a warranty (30 to 90 days is standard). You tell them what you need, they check inventory, pull it, and you pick it up or they ship it. Prices are higher than self-service, but you're paying for labor, testing, and a return policy.

Full-service yards are the better choice when:

  • You don't have tools or mechanical experience
  • You need an engine, transmission, or another component that's difficult to remove
  • You want a warranty and the ability to return the part if it's defective
  • You're buying for a customer's vehicle and can't afford to install a bad part

Which type is near you?

Search for "u-pull-it near me" or "pick-a-part near me" for self-service. Search for "auto recycler near me" or "used auto parts dealer near me" for full-service. Many cities have both types within reasonable driving distance.

What to Bring and What to Ask

Visiting a salvage yard without preparation wastes your time. Here's what experienced yard shoppers bring and ask.

What to bring

  • Your own tools. Self-service yards require them. Even at full-service yards, having a socket set in the truck lets you verify fitment on the spot.
  • Year, make, model, and trim level. Write it down or keep it on your phone. A 2014 Accord EX and a 2014 Accord LX use different parts in some cases.
  • The old part, if possible. Bring the broken one so you can compare side by side. Connector shapes, bolt patterns, and mounting points vary between model years.
  • Gloves and closed-toe shoes. Yards are full of sharp metal, broken glass, and fluids. Most self-service yards require closed-toe shoes for entry.
  • Cash. Some smaller yards still prefer cash and may offer a discount for it. All yards accept cards, but asking about a cash price is worth the question.

What to ask

  • "Do you have a warranty or return policy?" Get the terms in writing or at least confirmed verbally before you pay.
  • "Is this the original part or a replacement?" Rebuilt or aftermarket parts sometimes end up in salvage vehicles. You want to know what you're getting.
  • "Can you look up the interchange number?" Full-service yards with Hollander or Car-Part interchange data can tell you which other vehicles use the same part, expanding your options.
  • "Do you deliver or ship?" Many full-service yards ship parts regionally for a flat fee. If the closest yard with your part is two hours away, shipping may be cheaper than the drive.

How to negotiate

Salvage yard pricing is more flexible than most people assume. Here's what works:

  • Buying multiple parts from the same yard gives you leverage. Ask for a package discount.
  • Parts that have been sitting on the shelf for months are negotiable. If a part looks dusty, ask.
  • Cash discounts are common at independent yards. Ask, "Is there a cash price?"
  • If you find the same part listed cheaper on Car-Part.com at another yard, mention it. Many yards will match or beat a competitor's price to avoid losing the sale.

When to Go Local vs Online

The right answer depends on what you need and how fast you need it.

Go local when:
  • The part is common and readily available (headlights, mirrors, door handles, body panels for popular vehicles)
  • You want to inspect the part before buying
  • You need the part today and can't wait for shipping
  • You're comfortable removing the part yourself and want the lowest possible price
  • The part is large or heavy, making shipping costs prohibitive (hoods, doors, bumper assemblies)
Search online when:
  • The part is uncommon, discontinued, or for an older vehicle
  • No local yard has the vehicle in stock
  • You want to compare prices across multiple yards and regions
  • You need the part shipped to a repair shop or your home
  • You're looking for a specific trim-level or option-package variant

Many searches start local and go online when the local yards come up empty. That's normal. Start with the yard 10 minutes away. If they don't have it, search Car-Part.com. If that doesn't produce a result, try a voice broadcast through Hotline HQ or browse the methods in our online parts-finding guide.

For pricing benchmarks before you buy, our used auto parts pricing guide covers what to expect across common part categories.

Salvage Yard Hotspots by Region

Not all states are created equal when it comes to used parts availability. Vehicle registrations, climate, accident rates, and the age of the vehicle fleet all affect how many yards operate and what they stock.

California

The largest market for used auto parts in the US. California has over 800 licensed auto dismantlers, concentrated in the Los Angeles basin, the Inland Empire, and the Central Valley. The mild climate means less rust, which makes California yards a go-to source for body panels and structural parts shipped nationwide. Strict environmental regulations mean California yards tend to be well-run and compliant. See our full California used auto parts page.

Texas

Texas ranks second in the number of salvage yards, with heavy concentration in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, San Antonio, and the Rio Grande Valley. The Texas market specializes in trucks and SUVs -- Ford F-150 parts, Chevy Silverado parts, and Ram parts are always in stock somewhere. Hail damage in North Texas feeds a steady supply of late-model vehicles into the recycling pipeline. Our Texas page has more detail.

Florida

Florida's high accident rate and year-round driving season keep a large number of late-model vehicles flowing into salvage. The state has strong representation in yards carrying imports, especially Toyota, Honda, and Nissan. Coastal yards may have salt-air corrosion on some parts, so inspect carefully. Check our Florida page.

Arizona

Arizona is known for rust-free parts. The desert climate preserves body panels, undercarriages, and trim pieces in ways that yards in the Midwest and Northeast can't match. Arizona yards are a popular source for restoration projects and out-of-state buyers who need clean sheet metal. Many Arizona yards ship nationally. See our Arizona page.

Other notable regions

The Midwest (Ohio, Michigan, Indiana) has a high density of yards but rust is a significant factor on body parts. The Pacific Northwest (Oregon, Washington) feeds a steady supply of Subaru and Japanese import parts. The Northeast corridor (New Jersey, Pennsylvania, New York) has tight environmental regulations and high competition, which keeps pricing competitive.

Find the Part, Not Just the Yard

Knowing where the yards are is step one. Getting the actual part into your hands is step two, and the gap between those two steps is where most people lose time and money.

If you're searching for something specific, don't limit yourself to one method. Search Google Maps for what's close. Search Car-Part.com for what's in stock. Check your state recycler association for yards you haven't tried. And if you're still coming up empty, try a live voice broadcast through a network like Hotline HQ to reach yards that might have the part but didn't list it in any database.

The used auto parts market is big -- over $15 billion annually in the US, according to IBIS World (2025). The part you need almost certainly exists somewhere. The question is how quickly you can find it and at what price. Use the right tools, call ahead, and don't drive to a yard without confirming they have the vehicle in stock.

posts.bodyHtml:
If you need a used auto part and you want the best balance of price, speed, and reliability, your answer depends on who you are. Repair shops buying 20+ parts a week should be on a voice hotline network or running Car-Part.com searches in bulk. Individual car owners doing a weekend fix will get the most from eBay Motors or a local pull-a-part lot. Dismantlers sourcing from each other need a live network like Hotline HQ where 500+ yards hear the request at the same time.

There is no single best place to buy used auto parts. There are eight solid channels, each with different strengths. This guide walks through all of them — local junkyards, Car-Part.com, eBay Motors, Facebook Marketplace, voice hotlines, LKQ retail, RockAuto, and Amazon — and compares them on pricing, speed, reliability, and return policies so you can pick the right mix for your situation. For a deeper look at how to search for specific parts across these channels, see our complete guide to finding used auto parts online.

Key Takeaways
>
- Eight major channels exist for buying used auto parts, each suited to different buyer types and budgets - Self-service junkyards offer the lowest prices (40-70% below retail salvage) but require your time and tools - Car-Part.com indexes 200M+ parts and is the widest online search, though listings can be stale - Voice hotlines like Hotline HQ deliver confirmed-available parts with live pricing from 500+ yards in seconds - Always verify fitment by OEM part number, year/make/model/trim, and interchange database before buying - Combine two or three channels to cover both common and hard-to-find parts
Disclosure: This guide is published by Hotline HQ, which operates a voice parts network for auto recyclers. We cover every major buying channel honestly, including our competitors. Where we mention Hotline HQ, we identify it clearly.

Best Options by Buyer Type

Not every buyer needs the same channel. Here is the short version:

Repair shops and body shops running through parts daily need speed and confirmed availability. A voice hotline (Hotline HQ) or Car-Part.com gives you both. The hotline gets you a live answer and a price in seconds. Car-Part.com lets you compare listings across hundreds of yards at once. Individual car owners doing a one-time repair care most about price and return protection. eBay Motors and Amazon offer buyer-protection programs. Local pull-a-part lots deliver the lowest possible price if you're willing to pull it yourself. Dismantlers and yard operators sourcing inventory from other yards need a peer network. Hotline HQ's voice rooms connect you with 500+ yards simultaneously — you key up, describe the part, and yards with it respond in real time. That peer-to-peer dynamic doesn't exist on eBay or Amazon. See how auto parts hotlines work for a deeper look at the mechanics.

Local Junkyards and Self-Service Yards

Self-service junkyards — also called pull-a-part lots or U-Pull-It yards — remain the cheapest place to buy used auto parts in the country. You pay a small entry fee (typically $2 to $5), walk the rows, find your vehicle match, and pull the part yourself. Pricing runs 40% to 70% below what a full-service yard charges for the same part.

How it works

You show up with your own tools. The yard has rows of vehicles organized roughly by make or section. You find a matching vehicle, unbolt the part, bring it to the counter, and pay the posted price. Most self-service yards use flat-rate pricing boards — a door is one price, an alternator is another, regardless of make or model.

Pricing

Self-service yards are hard to beat on price. An alternator might run $25 to $40. A door assembly, $50 to $100. Engines and transmissions are priced higher but still well below full-service salvage pricing. For a breakdown of typical pricing across part categories, see our used auto parts pricing guide.

Speed and reliability

Speed depends entirely on your own hustle. If the part is in the yard, you walk out with it in an hour. If it's not, you've burned a trip. There is no way to check inventory remotely at most self-service lots. Reliability is as-is — you inspect it yourself, and there's no guarantee it works until you install it.

Return policy

Most self-service yards sell everything as-is, no returns. A few larger chains like LKQ Pick Your Part offer limited exchange windows (typically 30 days with receipt), but that's the exception.

Best for: Budget-conscious DIY owners, shops needing common body panels, and anyone who doesn't mind wrenching in a yard for an hour.

Car-Part.com

Car-Part.com is the largest online salvage parts database in North America, indexing over 200 million parts from thousands of recyclers (Car-Part.com, 2025). If a part exists in a participating yard's inventory system, it shows up here. For most people searching "used auto parts online," this is where they start.

How it works

Enter the year, make, model, and part name. The system returns matching listings from yards that have uploaded that part to their inventory management software. Each listing shows the yard name, location, price, mileage (when available), and sometimes a photo. You then call or email the yard to confirm availability and arrange purchase or shipping.

Pricing

Prices are set by each individual yard. You'll see a range of quotes for the same part from different sellers. This is useful for comparison shopping, but it also means you need to factor in shipping costs when buying from yards outside your area.

Speed and reliability

Search results appear instantly. The lag is in confirmation — a part listed on Car-Part.com may have been sold since the last inventory sync. Some yards update daily; others sync weekly or less. You won't know the part is actually available until you contact the yard. For hard-to-find parts, this step can eat time if your first three results are already sold.

Return policy

Return policies are set by each yard individually. Most full-service recyclers offer 30- to 90-day warranties on major mechanical parts (engines, transmissions) and shorter windows or no returns on body and electrical parts. Always ask before buying.

Best for: Shops and individuals searching for specific parts across a wide geographic area. The broadest net you can cast online.

eBay Motors

eBay Motors carries a massive volume of used auto parts from salvage yards, individual sellers, and parts resellers. It works well for both common and obscure parts because the seller base includes professional recyclers alongside individual car owners parting out vehicles.

How it works

Search by year, make, model, and part name — or by OEM part number for precision. Filter by condition (used, refurbished, new aftermarket), price range, and seller location. Most listings include photos, condition notes, and compatibility charts. You buy online and the part ships to you.

Pricing

eBay pricing is competitive because sellers undercut each other. You'll often find parts priced 20% to 40% below a local yard's asking price, especially for common components. Shipping adds cost, though — a $60 fender can carry $40 in freight. Watch the total landed price, not just the part price.

Speed and reliability

Shipping times vary from 2 to 10 business days depending on the seller and part size. Reliability depends on the seller's reputation. Check the feedback score and read recent reviews. Established sellers with thousands of transactions are generally safe. New sellers with thin histories carry more risk.

Return policy

eBay's Money Back Guarantee covers most transactions. If the part doesn't match the listing description or arrives damaged, you can return it. Some sellers also accept returns for fitment issues. This buyer protection is a real advantage over buying from a yard with no return policy.

Best for: Individual car owners who want buyer protection, comparison shopping, and shipping to their door. Also useful for shops sourcing rare or discontinued parts.

Facebook Marketplace

Facebook Marketplace and Facebook groups dedicated to auto parts have become a significant channel for buying used parts. The platform works best for local transactions — you search your area, find a seller, and meet up or arrange local delivery.

How it works

Search "used auto parts" plus your make and model, or join regional auto parts groups. Sellers post photos and prices. You message them, negotiate, and arrange pickup or meet. Some groups specialize in specific makes (Ford trucks, Honda Civic parts, etc.) and have active communities.

Pricing

Prices are all over the map. You'll find deals well below yard pricing from individuals parting out a vehicle who just want the car off their property. You'll also find delusional pricing from people who think their rusted fender is worth retail. Negotiation is expected.

Speed and reliability

Speed is fast for local deals — you can have the part the same day. Reliability is the weak spot. There's no standardized condition grading, no buyer protection, and no recourse if the part is bad. You're trusting photos and the seller's word.

Return policy

None. This is a private sale. Once you pay and take the part, it's yours. Some sellers will work with you if there's an obvious problem, but there's no formal process.

Best for: Local bargain hunters, people parting out specific vehicles, and anyone who doesn't mind spending time scrolling and messaging. Poor choice for shops that need consistent supply.

Voice Hotlines (Hotline HQ)

Voice hotlines are the fastest way to source a used part with confirmed availability and a live price. The Hotline HQ network connects over 500 salvage yards across the US in regional voice rooms. You describe the part you need into the room, and every yard on the line hears it simultaneously. Yards with the part respond immediately with pricing.

How it works

Yards join regional rooms organized by geography. When you need a part, you key up (like a two-way radio) and broadcast your request: "Need a 2019 Camry driver fender, any color." Every yard in the room hears it. If a yard has the part, they respond with a price and condition on the spot. Average response time is roughly 2 seconds. There are no search forms, no inventory databases to check — it's a live, real-time conversation between recyclers.

For the full breakdown of the mechanics, see our guide on how auto parts hotlines work.

Pricing

Pricing is yard-to-yard, negotiated live on the call. Because multiple yards may respond to the same broadcast, natural price competition happens in real time. You hear three or four offers and pick the best one. There is no Hotline HQ markup or commission on the parts transaction. The yard sells to you directly.

For context on what parts cost across the industry, check the used auto parts pricing guide.

Speed and reliability

This is where voice hotlines pull ahead. Speed is measured in seconds, not hours or days. And because a live person at the yard confirms the part exists right now, you avoid the stale-listing problem that plagues database searches. The part hasn't been sold out from under you — the yard just told you they have it.

Return policy

Return policies are between you and the selling yard. Most professional recyclers on the network offer standard 30- to 90-day warranties on engines and transmissions. Hotline HQ doesn't handle the transaction, so warranty terms are set by the yard.

Best for: Repair shops, body shops, and dismantlers who source parts daily. The speed and confirmed availability make it the primary channel for high-volume buyers. Individual car owners can benefit too, but the subscription model is designed for professional use.

LKQ Pick Your Part and Retail Locations

LKQ Corporation is the largest auto parts recycler in North America, operating both self-service (Pick Your Part) and full-service retail locations. Their scale means broad inventory and standardized processes — something smaller independent yards can't always match.

How it works

Pick Your Part locations are self-service. You search their online inventory tool to see which vehicles are currently in the yard, then show up, pull the part, and pay at the counter. Their website shows vehicle arrival dates, which helps you gauge whether the good parts have already been picked over. Full-service retail locations pull, test, and warehouse parts. You call or search online, they confirm availability, and you buy over the phone or in person. These locations ship nationwide.

Pricing

Pick Your Part pricing follows flat-rate boards — the same price for an alternator whether it comes from a Civic or a Cadillac. Full-service locations price by part and vehicle, typically at standard salvage retail rates. LKQ's scale doesn't always translate to lower prices, but their inventory depth means they often have the part when smaller yards don't.

Speed and reliability

The online vehicle inventory check for self-service locations is a genuine advantage — you can confirm a matching vehicle is in the yard before driving out. Full-service locations test major mechanical components, which adds a layer of reliability you won't get from a random eBay seller.

Return policy

LKQ Pick Your Part offers a 30-day exchange policy on most parts (with receipt). Full-service locations typically offer 30- to 90-day warranties depending on the part category. By recycler standards, their warranty program is among the most consistent.

Best for: Buyers near an LKQ location who want the convenience of a large chain with standardized pricing and return policies. Self-service for budget buyers, full-service for shops that want tested parts.

RockAuto

RockAuto is not a salvage parts source. It is an online retailer of new OEM and aftermarket replacement parts. It's included here because many people searching for "where to buy auto parts" consider it alongside used sources, and it's worth understanding where it fits.

How it works

RockAuto operates a massive online catalog organized by year, make, model, and part category. You search, add to cart, and check out. Parts ship from warehouses across the US. The catalog covers everything from oil filters to complete engines, with multiple brands at different price points for each part.

Pricing

RockAuto is consistently among the cheapest sources for new aftermarket parts. Prices often undercut local auto parts stores by 30% to 50%. However, new aftermarket is still more expensive than used OEM salvage for most major components. A new aftermarket headlight assembly might cost $80 on RockAuto vs. $40 for a used OEM unit from a salvage yard.

Speed and reliability

Shipping times run 3 to 7 business days depending on warehouse location and shipping method. Parts are new, so reliability is high — you're not gambling on unknown history. The trade-off is cost.

Return policy

RockAuto accepts returns within 30 days for most parts. Electrical parts and special-order items may be excluded. Return shipping is the buyer's responsibility.

Best for: Buyers who want new parts at the lowest possible price. Not a used parts source, but a practical alternative when the cost difference between new aftermarket and used OEM is small (wear items, filters, gaskets, brake components).

Amazon Used and Refurbished Parts

Amazon's auto parts section includes a growing selection of used, refurbished, and remanufactured components alongside new parts. The "Amazon Renewed" program covers some auto parts, and third-party sellers list used OEM pulls.

How it works

Search Amazon by part name, OEM number, or vehicle fitment. Filter by condition (new, used, renewed/refurbished). Third-party sellers handle fulfillment, though some use Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA) for faster shipping. Fitment accuracy depends on the seller's listing quality — always double-check compatibility.

Pricing

Pricing is competitive on common parts. Amazon's marketplace pressure keeps prices in check. However, the used auto parts selection is thinner than eBay's, and many listings are actually new aftermarket parts rather than genuine used OEM.

Speed and reliability

Prime-eligible parts ship in 1 to 2 days. Non-Prime listings vary. Amazon's A-to-Z Guarantee provides buyer protection similar to eBay's. Reliability of used parts depends entirely on the third-party seller.

Return policy

Amazon's standard return policy applies — most parts can be returned within 30 days. Amazon Renewed parts carry a separate guarantee. This makes Amazon a lower-risk option for used parts compared to Facebook Marketplace or direct yard purchases.

Best for: Buyers who already have Amazon Prime and want fast shipping with strong buyer protection. Selection is limited compared to eBay or Car-Part.com for used salvage parts.

OEM vs Aftermarket vs Salvage: Which Should You Buy?

Three categories of replacement parts exist, and choosing the right one depends on the component, your budget, and how long you need it to last.

OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer)

OEM parts are made by the same manufacturer that supplied the part to the automaker. A new OEM headlight for a 2020 Camry is the same part Toyota installed at the factory. New OEM is the most expensive option — often 2x to 4x the aftermarket price.

Used OEM parts from salvage yards offer the same fit and quality at 50% to 75% below new OEM pricing. This is the sweet spot for major components like engines, transmissions, doors, fenders, and headlights. The part was designed for your exact vehicle. It just has miles on it.

Aftermarket

Aftermarket parts are manufactured by third-party companies to fit the same application. Quality ranges widely — from budget brands with loose tolerances to premium brands that match or exceed OEM specs. Pricing sits between used OEM and new OEM.

Aftermarket works well for wear items: brake pads, rotors, filters, belts, hoses, spark plugs. For body panels, fit-and-finish can vary. A cheap aftermarket fender might need extra adjustment to align properly. For mechanical internals (engine gaskets, suspension bushings), reputable aftermarket brands like Moog, Dorman, and Denso deliver solid quality.

Salvage (used OEM from a recycler)

Salvage parts are used OEM components pulled from end-of-life vehicles by licensed auto recyclers. The part is genuine OEM — it just came off a wrecked or retired car. Salvage pricing typically runs 50% to 75% below new OEM.

The risk with salvage is unknown history. A transmission from a car with 120,000 miles has 120,000 miles of wear. Reputable recyclers test major mechanical parts and offer warranties. Less reputable ones sell as-is. Always ask about mileage, testing, and warranty before buying mechanical salvage parts.

For the parts in highest demand from salvage yards, see which parts dismantlers request most.

The rule of thumb: Use salvage OEM for major components (engines, transmissions, body panels, glass, lights). Use aftermarket for wear items and maintenance parts. Use new OEM only when no suitable alternative exists — or when the repair is on a newer vehicle still under factory warranty.

How to Verify Fitment and Avoid Bad Buys

Buying the wrong part wastes money and time. These steps reduce that risk significantly.

Match by OEM part number

Every major component has a part number stamped, etched, or printed on a label. Before you search anywhere, find the OEM part number for the part you need. Check the existing part on your vehicle, look it up in an OEM parts catalog (most manufacturer websites offer free lookup by VIN), or use a resource like RealOEM for BMW or Toyota's parts catalog.

When you find a listing, ask the seller for the part number on the unit they're selling. If the numbers match, fitment is confirmed. This is the single most reliable way to avoid buying the wrong part.

Use interchange databases

Not every matching part shares the same part number. Automakers often use the same component across multiple model years or across different models. Interchange databases like Hollander (used by most professional recyclers) and Car-Part.com's interchange lookup tell you which parts from other vehicles will fit yours.

For example, a 2018 Camry headlight might interchange with 2019 and 2020 model years. The interchange database confirms this compatibility. Without it, you're guessing.

Verify year, make, model, and trim

Trim level matters more than most buyers realize. A base-model Accord and an EX-L Accord may use different headlights, different bumper covers, different engines. Always specify the full trim level and engine size when requesting or searching for parts.

Inspect photos carefully

For online purchases, request multiple photos from different angles. Look for cracks, chips, corrosion, and mounting tab damage. On mechanical parts, look for oil leaks, corrosion on electrical connectors, and signs of previous repair. If the seller won't send detailed photos, move on.

Ask the right questions

Before buying any used mechanical part, ask:

  • What is the mileage on the part (or the donor vehicle)?
  • Was the part tested? How?
  • Is there a warranty? How long? What does it cover?
  • What is the return policy if the part doesn't work?
  • Is there a core charge?

These questions separate professional recyclers from fly-by-night sellers. A legitimate yard will answer all of them without hesitation.

Warranty and Return Considerations

Warranty coverage varies dramatically across buying channels. Knowing what you're getting before you pay saves headaches after.

Full-service salvage yards typically offer 30- to 90-day warranties on engines, transmissions, and other major mechanical parts. Some national networks offer extended warranties (up to 6 months or 1 year) for an additional fee. Body parts and electrical components often carry shorter warranties or none at all. Self-service yards sell as-is. You pulled it, you own it. A few chains like LKQ Pick Your Part offer 30-day exchange policies, but most independent pull-a-part lots do not. eBay Motors provides the eBay Money Back Guarantee, which covers parts that don't match the listing description. This is effectively a return policy backed by the platform, not the seller. It's one of the strongest buyer protections available for used parts. Amazon applies its standard 30-day return window to most auto parts, including used and renewed items. The A-to-Z Guarantee adds another layer if the seller doesn't cooperate. Facebook Marketplace offers no buyer protection for local pickup transactions. Once you hand over cash and take the part, your only recourse is the seller's goodwill. Car-Part.com is a search platform, not a seller. Warranty terms depend entirely on the yard you buy from. Always confirm before placing an order. RockAuto accepts returns within 30 days for most new parts. Return shipping is your cost.

If warranty matters to you — and for engines and transmissions it absolutely should — buy from a full-service yard with a written warranty, or through eBay or Amazon where platform-level buyer protection exists.

Where to Start

If you made it this far, you know there's no single best answer. The right channel depends on what you're buying, how fast you need it, and how much risk you're willing to accept.

For dismantlers trading with other yards, a voice network is the fastest and most direct path.

Whatever channel you choose, verify fitment before you buy, ask about warranties on mechanical parts, and don't let a low price on a mystery-condition part cost you twice when it fails.
