posts.bodyHtml:
The US auto recycling industry processes 12 to 15 million end-of-life vehicles per year, generates approximately $32 billion in revenue, and operates across roughly 9,000 facilities nationwide. It employs an estimated 100,000 to 140,000 workers. By weight, automobiles are the most recycled consumer product in the country — roughly 95% of retired vehicles enter the recycling stream, and about 80% of each vehicle by weight gets recovered and reused.

Those are the top-line numbers. What follows is the full breakdown: market sizing, yard counts, employment, environmental impact, regional distribution, and the forces reshaping the industry from EVs to inventory software. If you run a yard, are thinking about starting one, or cover this industry as a journalist or analyst, this is the reference page.

Key Takeaways
>
- The US used auto parts and recycling market is worth approximately $32 billion in annual revenue. - There are roughly 9,000 to 9,500 auto recycling facilities in the US, down from ~12,000 in the early 2000s. - The industry recycles 12 to 15 million vehicles per year — about 95% of all end-of-life vehicles. - Auto recycling recovers an estimated 14 million tons of steel annually, enough to produce nearly 13 million new vehicles. - EVs will reshape the industry over the next decade, but gasoline and diesel vehicles will dominate the salvage stream through at least 2035. - Technology adoption — from yard management software to voice-based parts networks — is widening the gap between modernized yards and those still operating on paper.

Headline numbers

Before the detail, here is the snapshot that matters for 2026.

MetricFigureSource
US used auto parts market size~$32 billionIBISWorld, ARA
Number of US auto recycling facilities~9,000-9,500ARA
Vehicles recycled per year (US)12-15 millionISRI, ARA
Estimated US employment100,000-140,000BLS, ARA
Percentage of vehicle recycled by weight~80%EPA, ANL
End-of-life vehicles entering recycling~95%ISRI
Steel recovered annually (US auto recycling)~14 million tonsISRI
Average revenue per facility~$3.2-3.5 millionIBISWorld
Global auto recycling market size~$70 billionGrand View Research
These numbers carry important caveats. The "market size" figure depends on what you count — parts resale, scrap metal, cores, fluids, towing, auction fees. The $32 billion number refers primarily to parts and materials revenue at the recycler level. The global figure includes all downstream processing.

Market size and revenue

The US used auto parts and recycling industry generates approximately $32 billion in annual revenue. That makes it one of the larger segments within the broader automotive aftermarket, which the Auto Care Association sizes at over $400 billion including new parts, service, and repair.

Revenue breaks down roughly as follows:

  • Parts resale: 50-60% of revenue for full-service dismantlers. This includes mechanical parts (engines, transmissions, starters, alternators), body parts (bumpers, fenders, doors, hoods), and electrical components. See our breakdown of the most-requested parts for real demand data from the Hotline HQ network.
  • Scrap metal sales: 25-35% of revenue. Ferrous metals (steel, iron) make up the majority by weight, but non-ferrous metals (aluminum, copper, platinum-group metals from catalytic converters) carry higher per-pound value.
  • Core sales: 5-10%. Remanufacturable cores — alternators, starters, rack-and-pinion units, engines — sold to rebuilders.
  • Fluids and miscellaneous: The balance. Recovered fluids (oil, coolant, refrigerant) and ancillary revenue like towing fees, storage, and wholesale brokering.

The $32 billion figure has grown steadily over the past decade, driven by rising vehicle complexity (more expensive parts to resell), higher scrap metal prices, and longer vehicle lifespans pushing more repair-age vehicles into circulation. Adjusted for inflation, real growth has averaged 2-3% per year.

Average annual revenue per facility sits around $3.2 to $3.5 million, but the distribution is heavily skewed. The top 10% of operators — many of them multi-location chains like LKQ, Pull-A-Part, and Pick-n-Pull — account for a disproportionate share. Small single-location yards may operate at $500,000 to $1.5 million. The median is lower than the mean.

How many salvage yards in the US

The Automotive Recyclers Association (ARA) estimates there are approximately 9,000 to 9,500 auto recycling facilities in the United States. This number has been declining for two decades. In the early 2000s, the count was closer to 12,000. In the 1990s, some estimates ran as high as 15,000.

The decline reflects several overlapping forces:

Consolidation. Large operators have been acquiring smaller yards. LKQ Corporation alone operates hundreds of locations. Regional chains with 5-20 locations have absorbed many independents. Consolidation brings economies of scale in purchasing, inventory management, and online sales. Environmental regulation. Stormwater permits, hazardous waste handling requirements, and state-level environmental compliance have raised the cost of operating a yard. Older facilities on unprepared land face remediation costs that can exceed the property value. Some states require financial assurance (bonds or insurance) for environmental liability. Land costs. Salvage yards need acreage, and they typically sit on land zoned industrial or agricultural. As metro areas expand, that land becomes more valuable for development. Yards on the urban fringe face pressure to sell and relocate — or close entirely. Attrition without succession. Many yards are family-owned, second or third generation. When the current operator retires without a willing successor, the business closes. This is one of the largest single drivers of yard count decline that rarely shows up in industry reports.

Despite the shrinking count, the surviving yards are generally larger, better capitalized, and more productive than the ones they replaced. Total industry revenue has grown even as the number of facilities has fallen, meaning revenue per yard has increased significantly.

How many vehicles get recycled each year

The US auto recycling industry processes between 12 and 15 million end-of-life vehicles annually. The Insurance Institute for Scrap Recycling Industries (ISRI) and ARA both cite figures in this range. The exact number fluctuates with new vehicle sales (which affect trade-in volume), average vehicle age, insurance total-loss rates, and scrap metal prices.

To put that in perspective: the US has roughly 290 million registered vehicles. Annual new vehicle sales run around 15 to 16 million. So the recycling rate roughly matches the replacement rate — the fleet turns over, and the recycling industry absorbs the outflow.

Not all 12-15 million vehicles go through traditional dismantlers. The flow looks roughly like this:

  1. Insurance total-losses and trade-ins enter the system through salvage auctions (Copart, IAA). Full-service dismantlers buy vehicles here, dismantle them for parts, and sell the remaining hulk to shredders.
  2. Self-service yards acquire vehicles from the public, auctions, and towing companies. Customers pull their own parts. After a vehicle has been picked over, the yard crushes and sells it as scrap.
  3. Direct-to-shredder vehicles skip the dismantling step entirely. These are typically vehicles with minimal parts value — heavily damaged, very old, or already stripped.

Roughly 80% of a vehicle by weight is recycled. Ferrous metals (steel and iron) account for the largest share. Aluminum has grown as automakers use more of it in body panels and engine components. Copper wiring, platinum-group metals from catalytic converters, and lead from batteries round out the recoverable metals.

The remaining 20% is auto shredder residue (ASR) — a mix of plastics, rubber, foam, glass, fabric, and dirt. ASR has historically gone to landfill, but new separation technologies and pyrolysis processes are improving recovery rates. The EU's End-of-Life Vehicles Directive targets 95% recovery by weight, and US recyclers are watching that standard closely.

Employment and workforce

Auto recycling employs an estimated 100,000 to 140,000 workers in the US. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) tracks employment under NAICS codes that partially overlap with the industry — motor vehicle parts (used) merchant wholesalers (423140) and scrap metal recycling. ARA's own surveys put the number toward the higher end of this range when including all facility types and related services.

The workforce breaks down across several roles:

  • Dismantlers and technicians — pulling parts, testing components, cataloging inventory. This is skilled work. A good dismantler knows which parts have resale value, how to remove them without damage, and how to identify interchangeable parts across model years.
  • Sales and customer service — handling walk-in customers, phone inquiries, and online orders. In network-connected yards, this includes managing requests through parts hotlines and online marketplaces.
  • Yard operations — receiving vehicles, moving inventory with forklifts and loaders, crushing and baling scrap, managing hazardous materials.
  • Administrative and management — purchasing vehicles at auction, compliance, bookkeeping, and increasingly, managing e-commerce and digital inventory systems.

The industry faces a workforce challenge. The work is physically demanding, sometimes hazardous, and carries stigma that makes recruiting difficult. Average wages for dismantlers and yard workers run $15 to $22 per hour depending on region, below what competing industries like construction and logistics pay. Skilled dismantlers who can handle electronics, airbags, and now EV batteries command premiums, but they are hard to find.

Parts reuse vs. scrap and shred

Not every vehicle that enters a yard gets the same treatment. The split between parts reuse and scrap/shred determines profitability, and it varies widely by facility type.

Full-service dismantlers prioritize parts recovery. A well-run full-service operation pulls 200 to 350 parts per vehicle, catalogs them in an inventory management system, and sells them through multiple channels — walk-in, phone, online, and voice networks. The remaining hulk goes to a shredder. Parts revenue per vehicle can range from $1,500 to $4,000 for a desirable late-model car or truck. Self-service yards let customers pull their own parts and charge flat or per-part fees. Parts recovery per vehicle is lower — customers take the easy, high-value items and leave the rest. But labor costs are dramatically lower. Self-service yards make their money on volume and scrap. Industry-wide, the data suggests that roughly 25-30% of a vehicle's parts by count are resold or remanufactured. The rest is scrapped. By revenue, parts resale dominates — a single engine or transmission can be worth more than the scrap value of the entire remaining vehicle.

The economic incentive is clear: maximizing parts recovery before scrapping is the highest-margin strategy. But it requires labor, inventory systems, and sales channels. This is why technology adoption and network connectivity — being able to find a buyer for a part quickly — matters so much. A part sitting on a shelf for a year is inventory carrying cost. A part sold within days of dismantling is pure margin.

Environmental impact

Auto recycling is one of the most impactful recycling industries by volume. The numbers are significant:

  • Steel: US auto recycling recovers an estimated 14 million tons of steel annually, according to ISRI. That is enough to produce nearly 13 million new cars. Recycled steel requires 60-74% less energy to produce than virgin steel.
  • Aluminum: An increasing share as vehicle aluminum content grows. Recycling aluminum saves 95% of the energy needed for primary production.
  • Oil: Recyclers drain and recover used motor oil, transmission fluid, and other lubricants. The EPA estimates that auto recyclers recover over 90 million gallons of used oil per year, which is re-refined or used as fuel.
  • Batteries: Lead-acid batteries are one of the most recycled products in the US, with a recycling rate above 99%. Auto recyclers are a primary collection point.
  • Tires: Roughly 30-40 million tires come off end-of-life vehicles annually. These enter the tire recycling stream for crumb rubber, tire-derived fuel, or civil engineering applications.
  • Refrigerants: CFC and HFC refrigerants are captured and either recycled or properly destroyed, preventing ozone-depleting and greenhouse gas emissions.
  • Mercury switches: Older vehicles contain mercury in convenience lighting switches. ARA and the EPA have partnered on collection programs that have recovered millions of switches.

The net effect is substantial. Auto recycling prevents an estimated 85 million barrels of oil equivalent in energy savings annually through materials recovery. It keeps roughly 27 million tons of material out of landfills each year.

The environmental story is also a regulatory one. Yards that fail to properly handle hazardous materials — oil, coolant, refrigerants, lead, mercury — face enforcement action, fines, and remediation orders. The industry's environmental credibility depends on proper practices at every facility, and it is one reason environmental regulation, while costly, has ultimately strengthened the surviving operators.

Where the yards are: regional concentration

Auto recycling facilities are not evenly distributed across the US. Concentration follows population, vehicle density, and climate.

The states with the most auto recycling facilities include:

StateEstimated yardsWhy
Texas800+Large state, huge vehicle fleet, major auction hubs
California700+Largest vehicle population in the US
Florida500+High accident rates, salt air corrosion, large retiree fleet
Pennsylvania400+Rust belt, older vehicle fleet, strong industrial base
Ohio350+Rust belt corridor, central logistics
New York300+Dense metro areas, high collision volume
Georgia250+Growing Sun Belt population, major auction centers
Arizona200+Sun Belt growth, low-rust vehicles (premium in other regions)
Sun Belt states — Texas, Florida, Arizona, Georgia — have seen yard growth as population shifts south and west. These states also produce vehicles with minimal rust, which makes their parts more valuable to buyers in northern states where salt causes body panel corrosion.

Rust Belt states — Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana — maintain high yard counts because their aging, rust-prone fleets generate steady end-of-life vehicle volume. But the parts themselves are less valuable for resale (rust damage), so these yards tend to be more scrap-heavy.

California is unique. Strict environmental regulation (DTSC oversight, stormwater requirements, CUPA compliance) has driven out marginal operators, but the remaining yards are large, well-run, and serve the nation's biggest vehicle market.

Regional dynamics directly affect how yards source and sell parts. A yard in Arizona can sell rust-free body panels at a premium to collision shops in Michigan. A yard in Texas can source late-model trucks totaled in hailstorms and sell parts nationwide. Network tools — including voice-based parts hotlines that connect yards across regions — make this cross-regional trade practical.

How EVs are changing the industry

Electric vehicles represented roughly 9% of new US vehicle sales in 2025 and are projected to reach 15-20% by 2030. For the salvage yard industry, the EV transition is simultaneously a threat and an opportunity — but the timeline matters more than the headlines suggest.

The slow wave

The average age of a vehicle at end-of-life in the US is approximately 12 to 15 years. EVs sold in meaningful volume starting around 2018-2020. That means the first large wave of end-of-life EVs will not hit salvage yards until roughly 2030-2035. For the next several years, the overwhelming majority of vehicles entering the recycling stream will remain gasoline and diesel powered.

This gives the industry time to prepare — but not unlimited time.

What changes with EVs

Fewer mechanical wear parts. EVs have no engine, transmission, exhaust system, starter, alternator, or conventional fuel system. These parts represent a significant portion of traditional parts resale revenue. An EV has roughly 70% fewer moving parts than a comparable ICE vehicle. Battery handling. EV battery packs are large, heavy (800 to 1,400 lbs for a typical pack), contain hazardous materials, and carry high-voltage risks. Dismantling an EV battery requires specialized training, equipment, and safety protocols. Several industry groups — including ARA and the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) — are developing standardized procedures. New high-value components. EV drivetrains include components with significant resale value: electric motors, inverters, onboard chargers, DC-DC converters, battery management systems, and individual battery modules. A salvageable battery module from a Tesla Model 3 can sell for $2,000 to $5,000 depending on capacity and health. Second-life battery market. Degraded EV batteries that no longer meet automotive performance standards (typically below 70-80% of original capacity) still have years of useful life in stationary energy storage. The second-life battery market is projected to reach $4-6 billion globally by 2030. Salvage yards that can test, grade, and sell battery modules into this market will find a new revenue stream.

What stays the same

EVs still have body panels, glass, interior components, suspension parts, brakes, wheels, tires, HVAC systems (minus the compressor drive), and electronics. Collision-damaged EVs generate the same demand for body parts that ICE vehicles do. Tesla body panels, for example, are already among the more expensive parts in the salvage market.

The yards best positioned for the EV transition are those already investing in technology, training, and diversified sales channels. The ones at risk are small operators who lack the capital for battery handling equipment and training.

Technology adoption in salvage yards

The gap between technologically modern yards and paper-based operations has never been wider. Technology adoption is reshaping how parts are inventoried, priced, found, and sold.

Inventory management systems

Modern yards use electronic inventory systems that catalog every part pulled from a vehicle — make, model, year, interchange numbers, condition, location in the yard, and price. Leading platforms include Pinnacle, Hollander, and Checkmate. These systems connect to online marketplaces (Car-Part.com, eBay Motors, PartCycle) for automated listing.

A yard without an inventory system is invisible to online buyers. Given that online and phone sales now account for 30-50% of parts revenue at connected yards, this is not optional for competitive operations. For a comparison of available platforms, see our salvage yard software guide.

Voice networks and parts hotlines

Before the internet, yards found parts for customers by calling other yards on the phone. That model never went away — it evolved. Modern parts hotlines connect hundreds of yards on a shared voice network. A yard broadcasts a parts request and every connected yard hears it simultaneously. If someone has the part, they respond in seconds.

This is the model behind Hotline HQ. It works because not every part is listed in an inventory system, and not every yard is set up for online sales. Voice networks fill the gap, especially for hard-to-find parts and yards that prefer phone-based selling.

Online marketplaces

Car-Part.com remains the dominant B2B and B2C marketplace for used auto parts, with millions of parts listed from thousands of yards. eBay Motors serves a large consumer market. Newer platforms like PartCycle and Row52 (for self-service yards) have carved out niches.

The trend is toward multi-channel selling: a part is listed in the yard's inventory system, syndicated to one or more online marketplaces, available through voice network broadcasts, and sold to walk-in customers. The yards that sell fastest are the ones visible in the most places.

Vehicle acquisition tools

Salvage auctions have moved almost entirely online. Copart and IAA (Insurance Auto Auctions) run the two largest platforms. Yards bid on vehicles remotely, using condition reports, photos, and estimated parts value to set their maximum bids. Sophisticated buyers use data tools to calculate expected parts revenue per vehicle before bidding.

Growth trends and projections

The US auto recycling industry is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 3-5% through 2030. Several structural factors support this trajectory.

Aging vehicle fleet. The average age of vehicles on US roads hit 12.6 years in 2024 and continues to climb. Older vehicles need more repairs, and used parts become more cost-effective relative to new OEM parts as vehicles age. This is the single most important demand driver for the used parts market. Rising new parts prices. OEM parts prices have increased 20-30% over the past five years due to supply chain costs, vehicle complexity, and inflationary pressure. The wider the gap between new and used parts prices, the stronger the demand for recycled parts. Insurance companies, collision shops, and consumers all have incentive to use quality recycled parts. Parts complexity and value. Modern vehicles contain more electronic modules, sensors, cameras, and driver-assistance components. These parts are expensive new and retain high resale value used. A radar sensor for adaptive cruise control, a 360-degree camera module, or an electronic power steering rack can sell for 40-70% of OEM price in used condition. Sustainability pressure. Corporate and regulatory emphasis on circular economy practices benefits auto recyclers. Insurance companies increasingly mandate or incentivize recycled parts use. Some states require collision shops to offer recycled parts options. The industry's environmental credentials — when backed by proper practices — align with broader sustainability trends. Headwinds to watch:
  • EV transition reducing traditional parts inventory (long-term)
  • Consolidation pressuring independent operators
  • Labor shortages in dismantling and technical roles
  • Scrap metal price volatility affecting the scrap revenue floor
  • Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) potentially reducing accident frequency over time, which would lower total-loss volume

The net outlook is moderately positive. The industry will grow, but the growth will not be distributed evenly. Technologically equipped, well-capitalized operations will capture most of it. Marginal operators without digital sales channels, inventory systems, or network connectivity will continue to exit.

What this means for yard operators

If you are running a salvage yard or considering entering the business, these statistics point to a few clear conclusions.

The market is large and growing, but consolidating. Fewer yards are splitting a bigger pie. The operators who survive and grow are the ones investing in technology, training, and sales channels. Paper-based operations with no online presence are on borrowed time. Parts resale is the margin play. Scrap provides a revenue floor, but parts resale is where the margin lives. Maximizing parts recovery per vehicle — pulling more parts, cataloging them properly, and getting them in front of buyers quickly — is the single highest-leverage activity in the business. Network effects matter. A yard that sells only to walk-in customers is leaving money on the shelf. Online marketplaces, voice networks, and regional relationships multiply your effective customer base. The data on most-requested parts shows what buyers are actively looking for right now. EV preparation is a medium-term priority. You do not need to retrofit your entire operation for EVs today. But you should be tracking the training requirements, understanding battery handling basics, and watching for the first salvage-title EVs showing up at auction in volume. The yards that start learning now will have a two to three year head start when the wave arrives. Workforce is a competitive advantage. In an industry where everyone struggles to hire, the yard that can attract and retain skilled dismantlers, train them on modern vehicles, and offer reasonable wages will outperform. Good people are harder to find than good vehicles.

The auto recycling industry has survived — and thrived through — every disruption of the past century: the shift from full-frame to unibody construction, the introduction of electronics, the rise of online commerce, and increasingly strict environmental regulation. The EV transition and continued consolidation are the next chapter, not the final one.

faq.q: What is the most valuable part to pull from a junkyard car?
faq.a: Catalytic converters are typically the single most valuable component by weight, selling for $200 to $1,500 depending on the precious metals inside. However, complete engines and transmissions generate the highest per-unit revenue at $500 to $3,500. For yards looking at total revenue per vehicle, the engine plus transmission plus catalytic converter combination usually represents 50-60% of the car's total parts value.

faq.q: Are used ECUs and infotainment systems worth pulling?
faq.a: Yes. Electronic modules have become some of the most profitable parts in modern dismantling. A factory infotainment or navigation unit from a 2018-2024 vehicle sells for $200 to $800. Engine control units (ECUs) run $150 to $600. They are lightweight, easy to store, and increasingly expensive to buy new from dealers, which drives used demand.

faq.q: Which vehicles yield the most valuable parts?
faq.a: Full-size trucks (Ford F-150, Chevy Silverado, Ram 1500) consistently produce the highest total parts value per vehicle because their engines, transmissions, and body panels all command premium prices. Luxury vehicles (BMW, Mercedes, Audi) have high per-part value but slower turnover. Late-model Toyota and Honda vehicles offer the best balance of value and fast sales because demand never drops.

faq.q: How much can you make parting out a single car?
faq.a: A clean 2017-2020 mid-size sedan (Camry, Accord, Altima) yields roughly $2,500 to $4,500 in total parts revenue if you pull and sell every sellable component. Full-size trucks run higher, typically $4,000 to $7,000. These figures assume you sell through a mix of direct yard sales, hotline network sales, and online listings. Actual revenue depends on how many parts you successfully pull and sell before the hull goes to scrap.

faq.q: Do turbochargers hold their value as used parts?
faq.a: Turbochargers are one of the strongest mid-to-high value parts in the current market. Used turbos from common vehicles like the Ford EcoBoost F-150 sell for $300 to $800. Units from performance and diesel vehicles push higher, $500 to $1,200. New replacement turbos run $1,000 to $3,000 from dealers, so the used market stays strong because the savings are significant.

faq.q: What low-cost parts are still worth pulling?
faq.a: Starters ($30 to $150), alternators ($40 to $200), side mirrors ($25 to $150), and window regulators ($20 to $80) are all worth pulling because they cost almost nothing to store, ship cheaply, and sell consistently. A yard that tests and tags these small parts can move dozens per week. The margin per unit is modest, but the volume adds up and these parts require minimal shelf space.

posts.bodyHtml:
The highest-value parts at a glance

If you run a salvage yard and want to know what to pull first, here is the short answer. Catalytic converters, complete engines, transmissions, turbochargers, and factory infotainment systems are the five most valuable used auto parts by resale price in 2026. A single catalytic converter can bring $200 to $1,500. A running engine from a late-model truck clears $1,500 to $3,500. A complete automatic transmission sells for $500 to $1,500.

These five parts alone can represent over half the total revenue from a single vehicle. Pull them first, test what you can, and price them before you touch anything else on the car. The rest of this post breaks down 15 parts across three value tiers so you can build a pulling order that puts the highest-dollar items on your shelf fastest.

Key Takeaways
>
- Catalytic converters, engines, and transmissions are the three highest-value parts in any salvage vehicle. - Electronics (ECUs, infotainment, headlight modules) have surged in value as dealer replacement costs have climbed. - Full-size trucks yield the most total revenue per vehicle. Late-model Toyotas and Hondas offer the fastest turnover. - Group your pulls by value tier: high-dollar parts first, volume sellers last. - Testing and tagging parts adds 20-40% to resale value across every tier.

High-value tier: $500 and up

These are the parts that justify buying a vehicle at auction on their own. Each one can sell for $500 or more from the right vehicle in the right condition.

Catalytic converters — $200 to $1,500

Catalytic converters contain platinum, palladium, and rhodium. Those metals drive the price, not the converter's condition as an auto part. A converter from a 2016 Ford F-150 with a larger substrate and higher precious metal loading can sell for $400 to $800. Hybrid vehicle converters — especially from the Toyota Prius — run even higher, $600 to $1,500, because the cleaner exhaust means the catalyst degrades less over time.

A few things to know. Converter theft laws have tightened across most states. You need proper documentation proving the converter came from a vehicle your yard owns. Keep VIN records tied to every converter you pull. Buyers — whether recyclers or precious metal refiners — will ask for provenance, and legitimate buyers pay more than shady ones.

Pricing depends entirely on the specific converter model and current precious metal spot prices. Generic aftermarket converters are nearly worthless. OEM converters from trucks, SUVs, and hybrids carry the real value.

Complete engines — $500 to $3,500

Engines are the backbone of used parts revenue. A 4-cylinder from a 2017 Honda Civic or 2018 Toyota Corolla runs $500 to $1,200. V6 engines from mid-size trucks and SUVs land between $800 and $2,000. V8s from Ford F-150s, Chevy Silverados, and Ram 1500s push $1,500 to $3,500.

Mileage is the biggest price lever. An engine under 80,000 miles commands a 30-50% premium over one with 150,000+. Compression testing adds value — a tested engine with documentation sells for 20-30% more than an untested one. Full-service yards that include a 30 to 90-day warranty on engines capture the top of the range.

Diesel engines are a category of their own. A Cummins 6.7L from a Ram 2500 or a Duramax from a Silverado HD can sell for $3,000 to $5,000 in good condition. Diesel supply is tighter and rebuilding costs are steep, so used diesel engines hold their value better than gas equivalents.

For detailed pricing across all engine types, see our used auto parts pricing guide.

Transmissions — $500 to $2,000

Automatic transmissions from trucks and SUVs sit at the top of the range. A 10-speed automatic from a 2018+ Ford F-150 runs $800 to $1,500. The ZF 8-speed found in Ram trucks and several BMW models goes for $700 to $1,400. These are complex, expensive-to-rebuild units, and buyers would rather install a known-good used one than pay $3,000+ for a rebuild.

Manual transmissions sell for less — $300 to $700 for most sedans — but they move fast because the pool of available manual vehicles shrinks every year. CVTs from Nissan and Subaru fall in the $400 to $1,000 range, with Subaru CVTs trending higher because of AWD demand.

Transmissions are heavy. Factor shipping into your pricing if you sell online. Freight on a transmission runs $100 to $250 depending on distance.

Turbochargers — $300 to $1,200

The turbo market has grown alongside the shift to turbocharged engines in mainstream vehicles. Ford's EcoBoost lineup alone has put millions of turbocharged trucks and SUVs on the road. A used turbo from a 2.7L or 3.5L EcoBoost F-150 sells for $300 to $800. Units from performance vehicles — the Focus RS, Mustang EcoBoost, Subaru WRX — push $500 to $900.

Diesel turbochargers are even more valuable. A Garrett turbo from a 6.7L Powerstroke runs $600 to $1,200. New replacements cost $1,500 to $3,000 from dealers, so the used price stays strong.

Check the housing for shaft play and oil contamination before pricing. A turbo with no play and clean internals commands full price. One with detectable shaft wobble drops 40-60% or becomes a core for remanufacturing.

Infotainment and navigation systems — $200 to $800

Factory touchscreen head units have become one of the fastest-growing value categories in the parts market. A factory infotainment system from a 2019 Toyota RAV4 or 2020 Honda CR-V sells for $200 to $500. Units from luxury vehicles — the BMW iDrive, Mercedes COMAND, Audi MMI — push $400 to $800.

Dealer replacement cost is the driver here. A new factory head unit with navigation runs $1,500 to $3,000+ installed at a dealership. Used units from salvage yards cut that cost by 60-80%. The demand is steady because these systems fail, screens crack, and aftermarket replacements don't always integrate with the vehicle's other systems.

Pull these early and store them carefully. Screen damage kills the value entirely. Wrap them in bubble wrap, store face-up, and test them if you have the wiring harness to do so.

Mid-value tier: $100 to $500

Parts in this tier won't pay for the vehicle by themselves, but they stack up. A single car can yield three to six mid-tier parts, and together they often match or exceed the revenue from one high-tier component.

ECUs and electronic modules — $150 to $600

Engine control units, body control modules, transmission control modules, and ABS modules have all climbed in value. A used ECU for a 2018 Chevy Silverado runs $200 to $400. BMW and Mercedes modules push $300 to $600 because programming and dealer costs make new units painfully expensive.

These parts are small, weigh almost nothing, and ship for under $15. That combination — high value, low shipping cost — makes them ideal for online sales. The catch is compatibility. ECUs are often VIN-specific or require reprogramming, so buyers need to know exact fitment. List them with the full part number, VIN, and any programming notes.

Headlight assemblies — $100 to $500

LED and adaptive headlight assemblies from 2017+ vehicles have pushed used headlight values well above the old halogen days. A factory LED headlight from a 2020 Toyota Highlander runs $200 to $400. Adaptive LED units from German vehicles hit $300 to $500.

Dealer pricing is the reason. A new OEM LED headlight assembly from Toyota lists for $800 to $1,200. From BMW, $1,500+. Used assemblies at half that price sell fast.

Condition is everything. A clean lens with no moisture intrusion and no cracks gets full price. Hazed or cracked lenses drop the value by 50-70% or make the unit unsellable. Pull headlights early and store them where they won't get bumped. For more on headlight pricing by type, check our pricing guide.

Doors (complete) — $150 to $500

A complete door — shell, glass, mirror, regulator, handle, lock actuator — sells for $200 to $500 from a common vehicle. Truck doors sit at the high end because they are larger and more expensive new. A complete door from a 2019 Ford F-150 in the right color runs $300 to $500.

Color match is the key differentiator. A door in the buyer's exact color saves them a $300 to $600 paint job. Yards that photograph doors with clear color codes visible sell faster. Shells without glass or hardware drop to $100 to $200.

AC compressors — $80 to $400

Compressors from common vehicles run $80 to $200. Trucks and luxury vehicles push to $250 to $400. Spring and summer are peak season — demand spikes as shops replace failed compressors before the heat hits.

Testing matters here more than almost any other part. A bench-tested compressor with a warranty sells for 30-40% more than an untested one. If you invest in a compressor testing rig, it pays for itself within a season.

Bumpers (OEM, painted) — $100 to $350

Bumpers are the most-requested part on the Hotline HQ network. A painted, undamaged OEM front bumper from a 2019 Honda Accord or 2020 Toyota Camry goes for $150 to $300 at a full-service yard. Truck bumpers — especially chrome ones from F-150s and Silverados — push $200 to $350.

The value is in condition and completeness. A bumper cover with no cracks, no missing paint, and all mounting tabs intact gets top dollar. One with a repaired crack or faded paint drops to $50 to $100 regardless of vehicle.

Hoods — $100 to $400

Steel hoods from common vehicles run $100 to $250. Aluminum hoods from trucks (the F-150 went all-aluminum starting in 2015) and luxury vehicles push $200 to $400. Aluminum is lighter, harder to repair, and more expensive new — all of which keeps used prices firm.

Dent-free is the standard. A hood with minor dents can sometimes sell at a discount, but most buyers want clean panels they can bolt on and drive.

Volume sellers: under $100

These parts won't impress you one at a time. But they are fast sellers, low storage cost, cheap to ship, and they add up across dozens of vehicles. Yards that systematically pull, test, and tag volume parts generate steady baseline revenue between the big-ticket sales.

Starters — $30 to $150

Most common starters run $30 to $80. Truck and SUV starters push $100 to $150. They are small enough to fit in a shoebox and ship for $10 to $15. Bench testing takes two minutes and adds $15 to $30 to the selling price. A yard pulling starters from every vehicle and testing them on a workbench can move 10 to 20 per week without trying hard.

Alternators — $40 to $200

Same profile as starters. Compact, shippable, steady demand. Standard alternators run $40 to $100. Heavy-duty and high-output alternators from diesel trucks hit $120 to $200. Remanufactured units compete in this space, so a tested OEM alternator with a warranty is your edge.

Side mirrors — $25 to $150

Powered, heated mirrors with integrated blind-spot indicators from 2018+ vehicles run $50 to $150. Basic manual mirrors sit at $25 to $50. Mirrors break constantly — parking lot bumps, side-swipes, vandalism — so demand never dries up. They are fragile, so pull them early and store them in bins with padding.

Window regulators and motors — $20 to $80

Not glamorous. But window regulators fail on every vehicle eventually, and new ones cost $100 to $250 from a dealer. A used regulator for a 2017 Honda Civic runs $25 to $50. Pull them when you strip the door, test them with a battery, and bag them with the motor attached.

Fenders — $50 to $250

Steel fenders from common vehicles run $50 to $150. Aluminum fenders from luxury vehicles push $150 to $250. Like bumpers, condition and color match drive the price. A dent-free fender in the right color is worth three times a damaged one.

What affects a part's resale value

Five factors determine what any used part is actually worth.

Year, make, and model

Newer costs more. A 2022 part sells for 40-60% more than the same component from a 2015. Luxury and European brands carry a premium because new replacement parts from those manufacturers cost significantly more. Common domestic vehicles — Civic, Camry, F-150, Silverado — sit at lower per-part prices but sell faster because the buyer pool is larger.

Mileage and wear

For mechanical parts — engines, transmissions, turbos, compressors — mileage is the primary value indicator. Under 80,000 miles is the sweet spot. Between 80,000 and 120,000 is average. Over 150,000 drops the value by 30-50% even if the part runs fine.

Condition and testing

A tested part with documentation outsells an untested one every time. Compression tests for engines, bench tests for starters and alternators, visual inspections for body panels. The time investment is minimal. The price premium is 20-40%.

Supply and demand

Regional availability matters. Truck parts cost less in Texas where F-150s and Silverados are everywhere. Import parts cost less in California where Honda and Toyota dominate. When a model gets discontinued or a recall hits, parts prices for that vehicle spike as the pool of donors shrinks. Watching live demand on a parts hotline network gives you a real-time read on what buyers need.

Market channel

Where you sell affects your margin. Direct sales through a yard or hotline network have the lowest overhead. Online marketplaces (eBay, Facebook Marketplace, Car-Part.com) add seller fees, photography time, and shipping costs — but they reach more buyers. For more on where to sell and the trade-offs of each channel, see our guide on best places to sell used auto parts online.

Which vehicles to prioritize

Not every vehicle at auction is worth the same in parts. Here is how to think about which ones to bid on.

Full-size trucks — highest total yield

Ford F-150, Chevy Silverado, Ram 1500. These three consistently produce the most total parts revenue per vehicle. The engine, transmission, and catalytic converter alone can clear $3,000 to $5,000. Add doors, bumpers, headlights, the infotainment system, and smaller components, and a clean late-model truck can yield $5,000 to $7,000+ in sellable parts.

Truck parts also sell faster than sedan parts on the hotline network. Ford is the most-requested make on the Hotline HQ network, and the F-150 drives most of that volume.

Late-model Toyotas and Hondas — fastest turnover

Toyota Camry, RAV4, Highlander, Corolla. Honda Civic, Accord, CR-V. These vehicles don't command the highest per-part prices, but they sell the fastest. Toyota and Honda parts rarely sit on shelves because the vehicles stay on the road for 15 to 20 years. When a 12-year-old Civic needs an alternator, the owner fixes it because the car has another 100,000 miles in it.

The combination of fast sales and consistent demand makes these vehicles low-risk auction buys.

Luxury and European vehicles — high margins, slower sales

BMW 3-Series and 5-Series, Mercedes C-Class and E-Class, Audi A4 and Q5. Per-part prices run 40-60% above domestic equivalents. An ECU from a BMW that sells for $400 might be $150 from a Chevy. A headlight assembly worth $450 from a Mercedes lists for $200 from a Toyota.

The trade-off is slower turnover. The buyer pool is smaller, and fitment is more specific. But if you have shelf space and patience, luxury vehicle parts deliver strong margins.

Hybrids — catalytic converter gold

Toyota Prius, Camry Hybrid, Ford Escape Hybrid. Hybrid catalytic converters contain more precious metals and degrade less because the gas engine runs less. A Prius converter can sell for $600 to $1,500 — sometimes more than the vehicle cost at auction. The battery pack is a bonus revenue source if you have the equipment and buyer connections to handle it.

A pulling strategy that maximizes revenue

When a vehicle hits your yard, the order you pull parts determines how much money you leave on the table. Here is a practical sequence based on value per minute of labor.

First pass — high-value extraction (30 to 60 minutes). Catalytic converter, ECU and electronic modules, infotainment system, turbocharger (if equipped). These are the highest dollar-per-pound parts and the easiest to damage if you wait until the vehicle is partially stripped. Second pass — major mechanicals (1 to 3 hours). Engine and transmission as a pair if you have the hoist capacity, or individually. These are the biggest single revenue items and require the vehicle to be relatively intact for a clean pull. Third pass — body and lighting (1 to 2 hours). Bumpers, fenders, doors, headlights, hood, taillights. Pull these before the vehicle gets picked over. Photograph each panel with the paint code visible. Fourth pass — volume parts (30 to 60 minutes). Starters, alternators, AC compressor, side mirrors, window regulators. Test on the bench, tag, shelve. These sell steadily and the pulling time per unit is minimal. Final pass — remaining value. Radiator, wheels and tires, seats, steering components, fuel pump. Anything left that's sellable before the hull goes to the crusher.

If you're looking for ways to sell more parts from each vehicle, a structured pulling workflow is the single biggest operational improvement most yards can make.

Where to sell high-value parts

Different parts sell better through different channels.

Hotline networks work best for parts with broad demand — engines, transmissions, bumpers, doors. When you broadcast a part on the Hotline HQ network, it reaches hundreds of yards instantly. No listing fees, no photography, no shipping logistics upfront. The buyer calls you and arranges pickup or freight. Online marketplaces are ideal for niche and high-value parts — ECUs, infotainment systems, turbochargers, specialty headlights. These parts have smaller buyer pools that benefit from national exposure. eBay, Car-Part.com, and Facebook Marketplace all work, but factor in seller fees (10-13% on eBay), photography time, and shipping when you price. Direct yard sales capture the best margins on common parts — starters, alternators, mirrors, regulators. Walk-in customers and local shop accounts move volume without platform fees.

For a deeper breakdown of where to sell and the trade-offs of each channel, read our guide on best places to sell used auto parts online. You can also explore our main sell used auto parts page for a quick overview of all seven methods.

posts.bodyHtml:
Here's the deal with the auto dismantler business. You buy end-of-life vehicles, tear them apart, and sell the parts for more than the whole car cost you. The Automotive Recyclers Association (ARA) estimates US yards process over 12 million vehicles annually, feeding a $32 billion used parts market (ARA, 2025). That number isn't shrinking. Average vehicle age hit 12.6 years in 2024, per S&P Global Mobility, and that keeps pushing demand for replacement parts dealers don't stock new anymore.

This guide covers how the business works from end to end. You'll learn how yards source vehicles, dismantle them, manage inventory, and sell parts through channels including auto parts hotline networks. If you're thinking about opening a yard, or looking to sharpen operations at one you already run, every section here is built on real numbers and industry experience.

Key Takeaways
>
- US auto recyclers process 12M+ vehicles yearly, feeding a $32B parts market (ARA, 2025) - Well-run yards can reach profitability within 12 months on $50K-$75K plus SBA financing - Five sales channels: voice hotlines, online marketplaces, walk-ins, social media, locating services - Licensing requirements vary by state but always include a dismantler license and environmental permits

What Does an Auto Dismantler Business Do?

An auto dismantler buys end-of-life vehicles, pulls the usable parts, and sells them at a fraction of new OEM prices. The industry employs over 140,000 workers across roughly 9,000 facilities nationwide, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS, 2024). It's one of the oldest recycling industries in the country, and one of the most profitable per square foot of yard space.

The core model is dead simple. Buy a car for $300-$800 at auction or from a tow-in. Strip every sellable part off it: engine, transmission, body panels, lights, electronics, interior trim. Sell those parts individually for a combined total that's 3x to 5x the vehicle cost. Crush the leftover shell and sell the scrap metal.

What separates profitable yards from the ones barely hanging on isn't the model. It's execution. Yards that move inventory fast, price accurately, and sell through multiple channels crush yards that rely on walk-in traffic alone. How much can you squeeze from each vehicle? That single question drives every decision in this business.

[IMAGE: Aerial view of an organized salvage yard with rows of vehicles sorted by make and model - search terms: salvage yard aerial organized auto dismantler facility]

How Do Salvage Yards Source Vehicles?

Salvage yards pull in vehicles through four main channels: insurance auctions, public auctions, direct tow-ins, and private purchases. Insurance auto auctions supply roughly 40% of vehicles entering the recycling stream, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS, 2024). The cost profile and part quality shift depending on which channel you're buying from.

Insurance Auctions

Insurance companies total out vehicles when repair costs exceed the car's value. Those cars go to auction through platforms like Copart and IAA. This is the most consistent supply channel for dismantlers. Expect to pay $200-$1,500 per vehicle depending on make, model, year, and damage type. Late-model vehicles with minor damage run higher because their parts move faster and pull bigger margins.

Public Auctions and Government Sales

County and city governments auction off abandoned, seized, and forfeited vehicles on a regular schedule. Prices tend to run lower, but vehicle condition is a coin flip. Some yards pick up 5-10 vehicles per month from these sales alone. Do your homework before bidding. Inspect every vehicle you can.

Tow-Ins and Private Purchases

Plenty of yards keep standing relationships with tow companies and body shops. When a car isn't worth fixing, the shop calls a dismantler who hauls it away for $100-$500. Some yards also buy directly from individuals through online classifieds or yard signage. These vehicles often cost less than auction buys, but volume is harder to predict.

[CHART: Bar chart - Average vehicle acquisition cost by channel (insurance auction, public auction, tow-in, private purchase) - source: ARA industry surveys and Hotline HQ network data]

From Whole Car to Sellable Parts: The Dismantling Process

A good dismantler can process a vehicle in 2-4 hours, pulling 200-400 sellable parts per car. The Automotive Recyclers Association reports that roughly 80% of a scrapped vehicle's weight gets recycled (ARA, 2025). The process follows a strict sequence designed to maximize part value and keep contamination out of the equation.

Fluid Removal

Every vehicle starts with fluid drainage. Engine oil, transmission fluid, coolant, brake fluid, power steering fluid, refrigerant, and fuel all come out first. No shortcuts here. EPA regulations require proper capture and disposal of all automotive fluids. Most yards run dedicated drain stations with built-in containment and separate tanks for each fluid type.

Part Removal and Testing

After draining, high-value components come off first: engines, transmissions, alternators, starters, and electronic modules. Every part gets inspected and tested where possible. Engines may get compression-tested. Transmissions get checked for obvious damage. Electronics get plugged in to verify function before they go on the shelf.

Body panels, lights, mirrors, and interior pieces come next. Order matters here. Pulling a door before the fender is easier. Getting the dashboard out before the seats gives you room to work. Speed counts, but so does care. A scratched bumper sells for less than a clean one.

What Remains

After the teardown, the stripped shell goes to a crusher. Crushed vehicles get sold to scrap metal processors at whatever the market rate is that week. Scrap typically adds $150-$300 per vehicle to the bottom line. In a well-run shop, nothing goes to waste.

[IMAGE: Auto dismantler removing an engine from a vehicle on a lift in an organized work bay - search terms: auto dismantler engine pull salvage yard shop mechanic]

How Do Yards Manage Parts Inventory?

Inventory management is what separates profitable yards from chaotic ones. A mid-size yard carries 5,000-15,000 parts at any given time, per ARA industry surveys (2025). Tracking what you have, where it sits, and what it's worth takes a real system. Relying on memory and handwritten tags doesn't cut it anymore.

Tagging and Cataloging

Every part pulled gets tagged with a unique identifier, vehicle source (year, make, model, VIN), condition grade, and storage location. Most yards run barcode or QR code systems tied to inventory software. Popular platforms include Pinnacle, Checkmate, and Hollander. The right salvage yard software pays for itself within months through faster lookups and fewer lost parts.

Storage and Organization

How you store parts affects how fast you sell them. Engines and transmissions go on racks, sorted by vehicle type. Body panels stand in organized rows. Small parts like alternators, starters, and sensors go into labeled bins. Walk-in customers need to find parts fast. Your crew needs to pull parts for phone and online orders even faster.

Inventory Turnover

Parts sitting 12+ months are costing you money in storage space and tied-up capital. Track what sells and what doesn't. If a part hasn't moved in 90 days, reprice it. At 180 days, it might be worth more as scrap than the shelf space it's eating. Why let capital collect dust? Smart yards watch turnover rates monthly and adjust pricing accordingly.

[CHART: Pie chart - Typical salvage yard inventory breakdown by category (engine/drivetrain, body panels, electrical, interior, suspension, misc) - source: ARA industry surveys]

Five Channels for Selling Salvage Parts

Successful yards don't rely on one sales pipeline. The US used auto parts market hit $32 billion in 2025 according to ARA, and that demand spreads across five distinct channels. Yards running all five capture revenue they'd flat-out miss otherwise.

Voice Hotlines

Live voice networks let you hear part requests from dozens or hundreds of yards in real time. Another yard needs a 2014 Ford F-150 tailgate? You hear the request on your desk phone and respond in seconds. The Hotline HQ network averages a 2-second response time across 500+ member yards in 12 regional rooms (Hotline HQ network data, 2026). For a deeper look, see our guide on how auto parts hotline networks work.

Online Marketplaces

Car-Part.com, eBay Motors, and Facebook Marketplace give you access to retail buyers nationwide. Listing parts online extends your reach well beyond your region. The trade-off: inventory data goes stale fast. A part you sold yesterday might still show available online today. Keeping listings current takes daily attention.

Walk-In Traffic

Local mechanics, body shops, and DIY car owners still walk into yards looking for parts. Walk-in customers typically pay full retail, making this your highest-margin channel. Good signage, a clean yard, and helpful staff keep them coming back.

Social Media

Facebook groups and Instagram work well for specialty and high-demand parts. Post a rare JDM engine or a clean set of OEM wheels and you can drum up interest within hours. Social selling means consistent posting, but the cost is effectively zero.

Locating Services

Third-party locating services connect buyers with yards for a fee or commission. These make the most sense for hard-to-find parts where the margin justifies the cost. Some services charge the buyer; others take a cut from the seller.

For a full breakdown of how to maximize each channel, read our guide on selling more parts.

[IMAGE: Salvage yard office with a desk phone connected to a voice parts network and a computer showing online marketplace listings - search terms: salvage yard office desk phone computer parts business]

What Licenses and Permits Do You Need?

Every state requires specific licenses to operate as an auto dismantler. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL, 2025), all 50 states regulate salvage vehicle operations, though the requirements look different everywhere. Count on needing a dismantler license, a general business license, and environmental permits at bare minimum.

Dismantler or Salvage Dealer License

Your state's DMV or equivalent agency issues this one. Applications typically require proof of a physical location, zoning approval, a surety bond ($10,000-$50,000 depending on state), and sometimes a background check. California's dismantler license calls for a $50,000 bond. Texas requires $25,000. Processing times run 30 to 90 days.

Environmental Permits

Handling automotive fluids, batteries, refrigerants, and tires puts you under EPA and state environmental agency oversight. You'll likely need a stormwater permit, a hazardous waste generator ID, and possibly an air quality permit if you run a crusher. Your state environmental agency's small business assistance program can walk you through the specifics for your location.

Zoning and Local Permits

Salvage yards run into zoning restrictions in most municipalities. You'll need property zoned for industrial or heavy commercial use. Some areas require buffer zones between yards and residential property. Building permits, fire department inspections, and signage permits may stack on top. Talk to your county planning department early. Zoning problems are the number-one reason new yard applications stall.

[CHART: Table - Licensing requirements comparison for CA, TX, FL, and AZ showing bond amounts, license types, and processing times - source: state DMV websites (2025)]

Environmental Compliance for Auto Recyclers

Environmental compliance isn't a paperwork exercise you do once and forget. It's an ongoing operational cost that protects your business and your neighbors. The EPA identifies improper automotive fluid handling as a leading source of groundwater contamination at small industrial sites (EPA, 2024). Proper fluid management, waste disposal, and stormwater controls aren't optional. Full stop.

Fluid Management

The average end-of-life vehicle holds 10-15 gallons of combined fluids: oil, coolant, transmission fluid, brake fluid, power steering fluid, gasoline, and refrigerant. Every one of them needs specific handling. Used oil and coolant can often be recycled through certified haulers. Refrigerant (R-134a or R-1234yf) must be recovered by a certified technician using EPA-approved equipment. Gasoline typically gets reused in yard vehicles or sold to fuel recyclers.

Hazardous Materials

Lead-acid batteries, mercury switches, and catalytic converters all need special handling. Batteries go to certified recyclers. Mercury switches found in trunk lights and ABS sensors on older vehicles must be removed before crushing per federal law. Cats carry value because of their precious metal content, but theft concerns mean proper documentation on every unit is a must.

Stormwater and Containment

Rain running through a yard picks up oil, metal particles, and other contaminants. Most states require a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP). That means covered fluid-handling areas, paved and bermed storage zones, and regular inspections. One spill incident can cost more in fines and cleanup than years of compliance investment. Worth the upfront spend? Every single time.

[IMAGE: Properly covered fluid drainage and containment station at a well-organized auto recycling facility with labeled tanks - search terms: auto recycler fluid containment station environmental compliance]

What Does It Cost to Start a Salvage Yard?

Starting an auto dismantler business takes real money, but the barrier is lower than most people think. The Small Business Administration (SBA) notes that small recycling businesses typically launch with $50,000-$75,000 in owner equity plus additional financing. A well-managed yard can reach profitability within its first 12 months of operation.

Startup Cost Breakdown

Here's where the money goes:

  • Land or lease: $2,000-$10,000/month depending on location and acreage. Rural properties cost less but draw less walk-in traffic.
  • Equipment: Forklift ($15,000-$30,000), fluid evacuation system ($5,000-$10,000), engine hoist, hand tools, and storage racks ($10,000-$20,000 combined).
  • Initial vehicle inventory: 20-50 vehicles at $300-$1,500 each ($6,000-$75,000).
  • Licensing, bonds, and permits: $5,000-$15,000 depending on state.
  • Inventory software: $100-$500/month.
  • Insurance: $3,000-$8,000/year for general liability, property, and environmental coverage.

Total first-year capital need runs $75,000 to $200,000. The exact figure depends on whether you buy or lease property and how aggressively you stock initial inventory.

Financing and Profitability

Most yards piece together personal savings with SBA financing. SBA 7(a) loans cover up to $5 million with terms up to 25 years for real estate. Some dismantlers start lean: lease property, buy 10-20 vehicles, then plow revenue back in to grow. Cash flow management is everything during those first six months while you're building inventory and customer relationships at the same time.

[CHART: Stacked bar chart - Auto dismantler startup cost breakdown by category (land, equipment, vehicles, licensing, software, insurance) - source: SBA guidelines and ARA industry surveys]

Plug Into a Regional Network

A dismantler business grows faster when buyers come to you. Hotline HQ operates live voice rooms across California, Texas, Florida, and Arizona, with a web dashboard for tracking every request that touches your yard.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to start a salvage yard?

Plan for $50,000-$75,000 of your own capital plus SBA financing. Total first-year costs typically run $75,000-$200,000 depending on property, equipment, and initial vehicle inventory. The SBA's 7(a) loan program is the most common financing path for new auto dismantler operations.

Do you need a special license to be an auto dismantler?

Yes. Every state requires a dismantler or salvage dealer license from the DMV or equivalent agency. You'll also need environmental permits, a business license, and a surety bond. Bond amounts range from $10,000 to $50,000 by state. California's is $50,000; Texas is $25,000.

How do salvage yards find parts they don't have in stock?

Yards use voice hotline networks, online databases, and direct calls to other dismantlers. On the Hotline HQ network, a single broadcast reaches 100+ yards at once with an average response time of about 2 seconds. Online databases like Car-Part.com offer broader reach but slower, less current results.

---

Look, this business hasn't changed at its core in 50 years. Buy smart. Pull clean. Sell through every channel you can reach. The yards making real money aren't doing anything exotic. They're just doing the basics faster and more consistently than everyone around them. Get your systems right, connect with buyers, and the numbers take care of themselves.

If you're ready to add a live voice network to your sales mix, see how Hotline HQ works for yard owners.

faq.q: Are online salvage parts databases accurate?

What is an auto parts hotline?

The US automotive recycling industry employs over 140,000 people across more than 9,000 locations, generating $32 billion in annual sales (Automotive Recyclers Association, 2025). An auto parts hotline is how many of these yards find and sell parts to each other in real time, without typing a single search query or waiting on hold. If you're new to the industry, our auto dismantler business guide covers how the whole operation works end to end.

Here's the basic idea. Members sit on an always-on conference room through a desk phone or web client. When a yard needs a specific part, say a 2019 Honda Civic front bumper, they key up and describe the ask. Every other yard in the room hears it instantly and responds if they've got it in stock.

This concept isn't new. Yards used radio networks and phone trees to locate parts for each other back in the 1990s. But radios were spotty. Coverage topped out at a few miles on a good day, and you couldn't reach yards two counties over.

Modern hotlines replaced all of that with internet-connected SIP phones delivering clear audio over dedicated conference bridges. The always-on model means yards don't need to call anyone. They just listen. When a request matches something sitting in their row, they answer. We've seen yards that were sitting on stale inventory for months suddenly move parts within hours of joining because they could finally hear the demand that was always there.

How does the voice network actually work?

Roughly 12 to 15 million vehicles reach the end of their useful lives annually in the United States, with about 26 automobiles recycled every minute (ARA, 2025). That's a massive flow of parts, and voice hotlines exist to match supply with demand in real time.

A yard joins a regional room. Could be California, Texas, Florida, Arizona, or one of eight other markets. Their desk phone connects to a conference bridge that runs around the clock. When a dismantler needs a part, three things happen:

  1. Broadcast. The requesting yard keys up and calls out what they need: year, make, model, and the specific part. That goes out live to every connected phone in the room. No typing. No waiting for search results.
  2. Listen. Every yard in the regional room hears the request through their desk phone speaker. Don't have it? Stay quiet. Simple as that.
  3. Respond. First yard with the part keys up and says so. The two yards connect directly to work out price, shipping, and pickup. No middleman sits between them.

The full cycle from broadcast to answer takes about 2 seconds on the Hotline HQ network. Compare that to calling yards one by one. That grind can eat 30 minutes to an hour just to reach 10 to 15 yards, and half of them won't pick up.

Our finding: On the Hotline HQ network, the average broadcast-to-response time is approximately 2 seconds across all 12 regional rooms, with the California room averaging 1.8 seconds due to its 200+ member density.

How do voice hotlines compare to other parts-finding methods?

Not all hotline networks produce equal results. After operating the Hotline HQ network for years, we've watched what separates a room that moves parts from one that collects dust on the counter.

  • Regional organization. Shipping a bumper from California to Florida costs more than the part is worth half the time. Grouping yards by geography keeps requests matched with yards that can realistically deliver or arrange a local pickup.
  • Low friction to respond. If you've got to log into a website or type out a message, you've already lost the sale to whoever picked up the mic. Voice wins because a yard hears the request and keys up to say "I have it" in the same second.
  • No commission on sales. Networks that skim a percentage on every deal give yards a reason to work around the system on big-ticket parts. Flat monthly pricing keeps incentives aligned. Dismantlers, salvage yards, and auto recyclers. These are businesses that buy end-of-life vehicles, break them down, and sell the usable parts. With around 9,000 locations operating across the US (ARA, 2025), they all face the same two problems every day.

As buyers: A customer calls asking for a part you don't carry. You've got two choices: lose the sale or find it somewhere else. On the hotline, you broadcast the request. Another yard in the region has it? You arrange a yard-to-yard sale and fulfill your customer's order. Sale saved. As sellers: You're sitting on parts nobody's asking about through your usual channels. By listening to the hotline, you hear every part request in your region. That transmission collecting dust for six months? Someone three counties over just asked for one. The hotline surfaces demand you'd never find through your website or walk-in traffic alone. A California yard doesn't hear Florida requests, and vice versa. That geographic focus keeps the signal-to-noise ratio high and ensures responses lead to actual sales rather than logistically impossible deals.

Setup takes minutes, not days. Sign up online, pick your regional room, and a preconfigured Yealink desk phone ships to your yard. Plug it in and you're on the live room, hearing part requests in your region as they're broadcast.

[PERSONAL EXPERIENCE] Yards we've worked with that added even one additional channel, typically a voice hotline, saw parts that had sat for 60 to 90 days sell within the first two weeks after connecting.

Pros:
  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero shipping costs
  • Cash transactions with fast payment
  • Builds long-term repeat customer relationships
  • Customers inspect parts in person, reducing returns
Cons:
  • Geographically limited to a 20-30 mile radius
  • Volume varies by weather, day of week, and season
  • Doesn't help move parts that local buyers aren't asking for
  • Hard to grow past the local market
Best for: Every yard benefits from walk-in traffic. It's your floor revenue. But relying on it alone means you're invisible to 99% of potential buyers.

Is Social Media Worth the Effort for Parts Sales?

Facebook Marketplace and local buy-sell groups have become a free sales channel for yards willing to post. Meta reports Facebook Marketplace reaches over 1 billion monthly visitors worldwide. Parts with clear photos sell, especially common items like engines, transmissions, and body panels. But results swing wildly from week to week.

The work itself isn't complicated. Post a photo with year, make, model, and price. Buyers message you directly. Some yards post 10 to 20 parts per week and see consistent inquiries. Others post the same volume and hear crickets. Facebook's algorithm decides who sees your listing. You don't control that, and it shifts without warning.

What about make-specific Facebook groups? They can work surprisingly well for enthusiast parts. A rare JDM engine or a classic Mustang fender gets more attention in a dedicated group than on any database. But the effort-to-return ratio is a coin flip.

Pros:
  • Free to list, no subscription or transaction fees
  • Reaches local consumers outside traditional yard networks
  • Make-specific groups attract serious, knowledgeable buyers
  • Photos and video help sell condition-sensitive parts
Cons:
  • Reach is entirely algorithm-dependent and changes without notice
  • Time-consuming to photograph, post, and respond to messages
  • Attracts tire-kickers, lowballers, and no-shows
  • No inventory management: sold parts stay posted until you remove them
  • Not designed for B2B yard-to-yard transactions
Best for: Yards with retail-friendly or specialty inventory and someone willing to manage posts consistently. Treat social media as a supplement, not a primary channel.

[UNIQUE INSIGHT] Social media works best for yards in metro areas where the local Facebook group population is large enough to generate real demand. Rural yards rarely see meaningful volume from this channel.

What About Parts Locating Services?

Parts locators act as middlemen between end buyers, usually repair shops, and salvage yards. Companies like PartsHotlines.com search databases of over 1,000 yards to match requests with available inventory. The locator handles the search and the customer relationship. But that convenience takes a real bite out of your margins. *(Note: Hotline HQ competes with parts locating services. We've tried to represent this channel fairly.)*

Most locators charge a per-request fee or take a commission on completed sales. Some pay you 30% to 40% below direct-sale prices. You're selling wholesale, plain and simple. The other issue is speed. Database-driven locating relies on inventory records that may be days or weeks old. By the time a locator matches your part to a buyer, a yard on a live network may have already closed that deal.

Pros:
  • Passive: the locator finds buyers for you
  • No listing, marketing, or sales effort on your end
  • Surfaces demand from repair shops that don't know your yard exists
Cons:
  • You sell at wholesale, typically 30-40% below direct prices
  • No relationship with the end customer
  • Dependent on the locator's network and effort
  • Stale database records can slow the match process
Best for: Moving slow-turning inventory that isn't selling through other channels. If a part has sat for 90 days with no matches on the hotline or your marketplace listings, a locator sale at a discount beats zero revenue.

Which Channels Should You Stack Together?

The most active sellers on the Hotline HQ network typically run two to three channels at once (Hotline HQ network data). No single channel covers all the demand for your parts. Here's a framework based on your biggest constraint.

Short on time? Hotline's the lowest-effort active channel. Plug in a phone, listen, respond when you've got the part. No listings, no photos, no algorithm games. Short on staff? posts.bodyHtml:
*Disclosure: Hotline HQ publishes this comparison. We've done our best to be fair and factual about all three networks. Where competitors do something better, we say so.*

Three networks, three models

If you run a salvage yard, three names keep coming up in parts network conversations: PartsHotlines.com, Car-Part.com, and Hotline HQ. Every yard owner hears about them sooner or later.

All three help you find and sell used auto parts. They just go about it very differently. PartsHotlines searches a curated database of member yards. Car-Part.com searches the largest inventory database in the industry. Hotline HQ skips databases entirely and connects yards on a live voice network.

Which one fits depends on what your yard needs most — reach, speed, or both. Here's how parts hotlines work at a fundamental level, and below is how these three stack up.

PartsHotlines.com

Founded: 1997 Network size: 1,000+ member yards Model: Database search with curated membership

PartsHotlines.com has been connecting yards for close to three decades. The model is simple: member yards upload inventory to a central database. A yard or buyer needs a part, they search PartsHotlines and get results from members that have it listed.

The network handles roughly 1.6 million searches per month. Yards are hand-selected for membership, so results tend to be higher quality than what you'd see from open-enrollment directories.

Strengths:
  • Large, established network with 1,000+ member yards
  • Hand-selected membership means results come from verified, operating yards
  • Nearly 30 years of industry relationships and brand recognition
  • 1.6 million monthly searches means real buyer traffic
  • Database search is familiar — works like any online parts lookup
Weaknesses:
  • Inventory data freshness depends on upload frequency. A part sold yesterday might still show as available today
  • Search results are only as good as the data yards submit. Incomplete uploads mean missed matches
  • Response isn't instant — a search returns listings, then you still need to call the yard and confirm
  • Buyer-seller communication happens outside the platform
Best for: Yards that maintain up-to-date inventory records and want passive exposure to a large, curated network of verified yards.

Car-Part.com

Network size: 200 million parts searchable Model: Massive inventory database with software integration

Car-Part.com is the largest used auto parts search engine in the industry. 200 million searchable parts — nothing else comes close in raw database size. The platform pulls inventory data from yards running compatible management software, especially their own Checkmate system.

Scale is the whole story here. A buyer looking for a 2017 Ford F-150 tailgate might see results from hundreds of yards across the country. That kind of breadth makes it the default first stop for a lot of parts buyers.

Strengths:
  • 200 million parts — the largest searchable inventory database in the industry by a wide margin
  • Broad geographic reach spanning the entire US and parts of Canada
  • Tight integration with Checkmate yard management software. If you run Checkmate, your inventory flows directly to Car-Part.com
  • High buyer traffic. Many repair shops and body shops search Car-Part.com first
  • Used by both professional yards and retail parts buyers
Weaknesses:
  • Data freshness varies. Inventory records are only as current as the last sync from a yard's management software. A yard that syncs weekly has week-old data
  • Size creates noise. A search can return dozens of results, and the buyer can't tell which listings reflect actual current availability
  • Yards without Checkmate or compatible software are going to struggle keeping listings current
  • Commoditizes parts — your listing sits alongside hundreds of others, competing on price alone
Best for: Yards that want maximum passive reach and are willing to maintain current inventory records. Strong for yards already running Checkmate or compatible management software.

Hotline HQ

Network size: 500+ yards across 12 regional rooms Model: Live voice network (always-on conference bridge)

Hotline HQ works differently from both PartsHotlines and Car-Part.com. No database. No listings. Yards connect a desk phone to an always-on conference room for their region. Someone needs a part, they key up and describe it. Every yard in the room hears the request and responds live if they have it.

Average response time on the network: about 2 seconds. That speed comes from the design itself — you're asking real people in real time, not searching records that may be hours or days old.

Hotline HQ operates in 12 regional markets, with the highest yard density in California, Texas, Arizona, and Florida.

Strengths:
  • Real-time communication. No data staleness — when a yard says "I have it," they're confirming availability right now
  • Average response time of ~2 seconds from broadcast to first answer (Hotline HQ network data)
  • Zero inventory uploading required. No software, no listings, no data entry. Plug in the phone and start
  • Regional rooms group yards by geography, so matches are typically shippable or even drivable
  • Flat monthly pricing with no commissions. The sale is between yards — Hotline HQ doesn't take a cut
  • Surfaces demand you'd never see. You hear requests for parts you didn't know someone needed
Weaknesses:
  • Smaller network than Car-Part.com or PartsHotlines. 500+ yards across 12 rooms vs. thousands in a database
  • Regional coverage only. If your market isn't in one of the 12 active rooms, the network doesn't reach you yet
  • Voice-based means you need someone in the yard listening. Not a passive system you can set and forget
  • No searchable online database for end consumers. This is a yard-to-yard network
Best for: Yards that value speed and accuracy over passive reach. Strong for yards that need to fulfill customer requests fast and want to hear real-time demand from their region.
